baseline_rows.pred_answer: The engagement-scoring feature would not fall into a risk tier at all, it is a prohibited AI practice. Article 5(1)(f) prohibits the placing on the market, putting into service for that specific purpose, and the use of AI systems to infer emotions of a natural person in the areas of workplace and education institutions. Inferring "engagement" from employees' facial expressions is exactly the identification or inference of emotions or intentions of natural persons on the basis of their biometric data that the Regulation treats as emotion recognition (Recital 18 being interpretive only). That the tool is internal, built by you and used only on the operator's own staff does not help: Article 5(1)(f) catches "putting into service" and "use", not just commercial placing on the market, and the operator's employees are in the workplace area the prohibition protects. Employee consent, anonymisation of scores, or using the output only in aggregate does not cure it, because the prohibition attaches to the inference itself rather than to any downstream decision, and no consent-based derogation exists in Article 5(1)(f). The single carve-out in Article 5(1)(f) is where the AI system is intended to be put in place or into the market for medical or safety reasons, for example fatigue or alertness detection protecting the health or physical safety of the worker. Productivity, attention, or meeting-engagement measurement is neither, so the carve-out is unavailable on the facts you describe. Only if a redesigned feature genuinely sat within that medical-or-safety exception would it cease to be prohibited, and it would then be an emotion recognition system falling under the biometrics area of Annex III point 1, with the full Chapter III high-risk regime applying (Articles 9 to 15, 43, 47 to 49, 72 and 73 as provider, Article 26 as deployer), together with the Article 50(3) duty on deployers of an emotion recognition system to inform the natural persons exposed to it of its operation, in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of first interaction or exposure and conforming to applicable accessibility requirements (Article 50(5)). The existing meeting-notes summarisation function is unaffected and remains outside the high-risk categories; the operator's Article 4 duty to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among staff operating it continues to apply. The compliant course is to drop the facial-expression engagement scoring entirely, or to replace it with a measure that does not infer emotions from biometric data.

A CV-sorting system used for recruitment falls under Annex III point 4(a) (employment, workers' management and access to self-employment), and is therefore high-risk under Article 6(2). Because it sits in points 2 to 8 of Annex III rather than in point 1 (biometrics), Article 43(2) applies: the provider must follow the conformity assessment procedure based on internal control set out in Annex VI, which does not provide for the involvement of a notified body. The notified-body route under Annex VII, and the choice between procedures under Article 43(1), are reserved for Annex III point 1 systems; they are not available or required here, and this is so regardless of whether harmonised standards under Article 40 or common specifications under Article 41 have been applied. Under Annex VI the provider carries out three steps itself (Annex VI.1): it verifies that the established quality management system complies with Article 17 (Annex VI.2); it examines the information contained in the technical documentation in order to assess the AI system's compliance with the essential requirements of Chapter III, Section 2 (Annex VI.3); and it verifies that the design and development process of the system and its post-market monitoring under Article 72 are consistent with that technical documentation (Annex VI.4). The technical documentation must have been drawn up before placing on the market and kept up to date, containing at least the Annex IV elements (Article 11(1)). Conformity is then demonstrated by completing the provider's Article 16(1) chain before market placement: ensuring the system undergoes the Article 43 procedure prior to being placed on the market or put into service (Article 16(1)(f)); drawing up the EU declaration of conformity in accordance with Article 47 (Article 16(1)(g)); affixing the CE marking to the system or, where that is not possible, to its packaging or accompanying documentation, in accordance with Article 48 (Article 16(1)(h)); and complying with the registration obligations in Article 49(1) by registering the system in the EU database (Article 16(1)(i)). The system must also be accompanied by instructions for use that state, among other things, the changes to the system and its performance pre-determined by the provider at the moment of the initial conformity assessment (Article 13(3)(c)). After placing on the market, the assessment is not final: a new conformity assessment procedure is required in the event of a substantial modification, regardless of whether the modified system is further distributed or continues to be used by the current deployer; changes to a continuously learning system that were pre-determined by the provider at the initial conformity assessment and are contained in the technical documentation under Annex IV point 2(f) do not constitute a substantial modification (Article 43(4)). Towards authorities, conformity is demonstrated on a reasoned request by supplying all information and documentation necessary to show compliance with the Section 2 requirements, in a language easily understood by the authority among the official Union languages indicated by the Member State concerned (Article 21(1)), together with access to the automatically generated logs referred to in Article 12(1) to the extent they are under the provider's control (Article 21(2)); such information is treated under the confidentiality obligations of Article 78 (Article 21(3)), which protect intellectual property, confidential business information and trade secrets, including source code.

Yes, at 3×10^25 cumulative training FLOPs the operator's model changes classification: it is presumed to have high-impact capabilities and therefore falls to be classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk, because Article 51(2) attaches that presumption whenever the cumulative amount of computation used for training, measured in floating-point operations (Article 3(67)), is greater than 10^25, which triggers Article 51(1)(a); the Commission may separately designate a model under Article 51(1)(b) on the Annex XIII criteria (parameters, dataset quality and size, training compute, input and output modalities, benchmarks and capability evaluations, reach among business users and EU end-users, registered users), and may amend the thresholds and supplement benchmarks and indicators by delegated act under Article 51(3). The presumption in Article 51(2) operates on high-impact capabilities as such; the underlying premise that the operator is a provider (Article 3(3)) of a general-purpose AI model (Article 3(63)) is assumed from the operator's own description. As to obligations, the compute figure does not displace the baseline Article 53(1) duties, which continue to apply in full: draw up and keep up to date the technical documentation of the model, including its training and testing process and the results of its evaluation, per Annex XI (Article 53(1)(a)); draw up, keep up to date and make available information and documentation to providers of AI systems intending to integrate the model, so as to enable them to understand its capabilities and limitations and to comply with their own obligations under the Regulation, containing at a minimum the Annex XII elements (Article 53(1)(b)(i), (ii)); put in place a policy to comply with Union copyright law (Article 53(1)(c)); and draw up and make publicly available a sufficiently detailed summary of the content used for training (Article 53(1)(d)). What the threshold adds is Article 55(1), which applies in addition to Articles 53 and 54: perform model evaluation in accordance with standardised protocols and tools reflecting the state of the art, including conducting and documenting adversarial testing with a view to identifying and mitigating systemic risks (Article 55(1)(a)); assess and mitigate possible systemic risks at Union level, including their sources, stemming from the development, the placing on the market or the use of the model (Article 55(1)(b)); keep track of, document and report, without undue delay, to the AI Office and, as appropriate, to national competent authorities, relevant information about serious incidents and possible corrective measures (Article 55(1)(c)); and ensure an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for both the model and its physical infrastructure (Article 55(1)(d)). Information and documentation obtained under Article 55, including trade secrets, is subject to the Article 78 confidentiality regime (Article 55(3)). The threshold also removes an exemption you would otherwise have: the Article 53(2) carve-out from Article 53(1)(a) and (b) for models released under a free and open-source licence permitting access, usage, modification and distribution with publicly available parameters, weights, architecture information and model-usage information expressly does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, so at 3×10^25 FLOPs the full Article 53(1) set applies irrespective of licence, while the copyright policy and training-content summary under Article 53(1)(c), (d) would have applied in any event. Pending publication of a harmonised standard you may rely on codes of practice within the meaning of Article 56 to demonstrate compliance with Article 53(1) (Article 53(4)) and with Article 55(1) (Article 55(2)); compliance with European harmonised standards confers a presumption of conformity to the extent they cover those obligations, and a provider that neither adheres to an approved code of practice nor complies with a harmonised standard must demonstrate alternative adequate means of compliance for assessment by the Commission (Article 53(4)). Two limits are worth stating. First, Article 51(2) creates a presumption, not an irrebuttable classification, it rests on Article 51(1)(a) high-impact capabilities as evaluated on appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks. Second, none of this makes the operator's model or any system built on it high-risk: high-risk status arises only through Article 6(1) (a safety component of, or itself, a product covered by the Annex I harmonisation legislation and required to undergo third-party conformity assessment thereunder) or Article 6(2) (a listed use-case under one of the eight Annex III areas), subject to the Article 6(3) derogation, so the Article 14 human-oversight and Article 27 fundamental-rights-impact-assessment duties are not engaged by the compute figure. Separately, the operator's Article 4 AI-literacy duty and, where the operator places an AI system intended to interact directly with natural persons on the market, the Article 50(1) disclosure duty, inapplicable where the interaction is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person, and disapplied for systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences subject to appropriate safeguards, unless those systems are available for the public to report a criminal offence, turn on the operator's activities rather than on training compute. If a third party later fine-tunes the operator's model, that modifier becomes a provider in its own right only on the Article 25(1) grounds where an AI system is concerned; below the relevant modification threshold the original-provider obligations remain with you.

Yes, the operator's legal role changes: by substantially modifying the model and placing the operator's own name or trademark on it, the operator becomes the provider of that high-risk AI system and cease to be a mere deployer. Article 25(1) attaches provider status to a deployer (or other third party) in three alternative cases, any one of which suffices: (a) it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service, without prejudice to contractual arrangements allocating obligations otherwise; (b) it makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service in such a way that it remains high-risk; or (c) it modifies the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, not classified as high-risk in such a way that it becomes high-risk. The operator's facts engage both (a) and (b) independently, so the re-branding alone would already trigger the change. The system remains high-risk throughout: AI systems intended to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score fall within Annex III, point 5(b), and Article 6(2) classifies Annex III systems as high-risk. The Article 6(3) derogation is unavailable to you, because a system performing profiling of natural persons is always high-risk notwithstanding the conditions in points (a) to (d) of that paragraph, and in any event you would have to document the assessment and register before market placement. As provider, the Section 2 requirements now fall on you for the modified system: a risk management system established, implemented, documented and maintained as a continuous iterative process across the lifecycle, with identification and analysis of known and reasonably foreseeable risks, estimation and evaluation of risks in intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse, evaluation of post-market-monitoring risks, and adoption of targeted measures such that residual risks are acceptable (Article 9(1), (5)); data governance over the training, validation and testing sets used in the operator's re-training, which must be relevant, sufficiently representative, to the best extent possible free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose, with examination for biases and mitigation measures (Article 10(1), (3)); technical documentation drawn up before the modified system is placed on the market and kept up to date, containing at least the Annex IV elements (Article 11(1)); design for operational transparency plus instructions for use containing the provider identity and contact details, the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance, intended purpose; accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity levels and metrics tested against; foreseeable circumstances leading to health, safety or fundamental-rights risks; explanatory capabilities; performance on specific persons or groups; input-data specifications; and information enabling output interpretation, the pre-determined changes, the human oversight measures, the computational and hardware resources, expected lifetime and maintenance, and the log-collection mechanisms (Article 13(1), (3)); built-in human-machine interface tools enabling effective oversight, with measures built into the system or specified for the deployer, enabling the overseeing person to understand capacities and limitations, remain aware of automation bias, correctly interpret outputs, disregard, override or reverse the output, and intervene or halt operation (Article 14(1), (4)); and appropriate accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity performing consistently across the lifecycle, with accuracy metrics declared in the instructions for use and resilience against errors, feedback loops, data and model poisoning, adversarial examples, confidentiality attacks and model flaws (Article 15(1), (3), (5)). The operator must also run a fresh conformity assessment for the substantially modified system, draw up the EU declaration of conformity, affix CE marking, operate a quality management system, register in the EU database and conduct post-market monitoring. Correspondingly, under Article 25(2) the initial provider is no longer considered the provider of that specific system, but must cooperate closely, make available the information and provide the reasonably expected technical access and other assistance the operator need to fulfil the provider obligations, unless it has clearly specified that its system is not to be changed into a high-risk AI system and therefore does not fall under that hand-over duty. Finally, to the extent you continue to use the system under the operator's own authority, the deployer duties in Articles 26 and 27 continue to bind you in parallel: use in accordance with the instructions for use, assignment of human oversight to competent, trained natural persons with the necessary authority and support, input-data relevance control within the operator's control, monitoring of operation with suspension and notification where risks arise, log retention, worker information, use of Article 13 information for any Article 35 GDPR data protection impact assessment, and informing natural persons subject to the system that they are subject to its use (Article 26(1), (11)); and, because credit scoring is an Annex III, point 5(b) use, a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use, covering the operator's deployment processes and intended purpose, the period and frequency of use, the categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected, the specific risks of harm to them, the human oversight measures to be implemented, and the governance, complaint and remedial measures to be taken if risks materialise, notified to the market surveillance authority (Article 27(1)).

Yes, the extension changes the classification. Scoring final exams and determining pass/fail is an AI system intended to be used to evaluate learning outcomes of natural persons in educational and vocational training institutions, which is a listed use-case under Annex III, point 3 (education and vocational training), whose lettered entries cover determining access, admission or assignment to institutions (a), evaluating learning outcomes including where they steer the learning process (b), assessing the appropriate level of education a person will receive or can access (c), and monitoring and detecting prohibited behaviour during tests (d). A system falling within any of those entries is high-risk under Article 6(2). The tutoring function as originally described, study support with an AI disclosure, is not itself a listed Annex III use-case; it is the assessment and pass/fail purpose that pulls the system into Annex III point 3(b). Annex I plays no role here: the product route under Article 6(1) requires the system to be a safety component of, or itself be, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and subject to third-party conformity assessment under that legislation, which an exam-scoring chatbot is not. The Article 6(3) derogation will not rescue it. The four conditions are a narrow procedural task, improving the result of a previously completed human activity, detecting decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns without replacing or influencing the previously completed human assessment without proper human review, or performing a preparatory task, and in each case the system must also pose no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights. A system that itself produces the score and the pass/fail outcome replaces rather than assists the human assessment, and a determinative educational outcome is a significant risk to fundamental rights. If the system profiles natural persons it is high-risk in all cases regardless of the conditions. Should you nevertheless take the view that it is not high-risk, Article 6(4) requires the operator to document that assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service, to register under Article 49(2), and to supply the documentation to national competent authorities on request. Because the operator is the provider extending the operator's own system's intended purpose, the full Article 16 provider set attaches: Section 2 conformity, the operator's name and contact details on the system or its documentation, a quality management system (Article 17), technical documentation and logs (Articles 11, 18, 19), conformity assessment before placing on the market (Article 43), the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47), CE marking (Article 48), registration in the EU database before placing on the market or putting into service (Article 49, national-level registration under Article 49(5) is reserved for Annex III point 2 systems, not education), corrective action (Article 20), demonstration of conformity on reasoned request (Article 21), and accessibility requirements. Article 15 additionally requires appropriate accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity consistently across the lifecycle, with the accuracy levels and metrics declared in the instructions for use, resilience against errors, faults and inconsistencies including through redundancy or fail-safe plans, mitigation of feedback loops where the system continues to learn after deployment, and resilience against unauthorised third-party alteration of its use, outputs or performance. Note the value-chain consequence if the change is made by someone else: under Article 25(1)(c), a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party that modifies the intended purpose of an already-marketed system so that it becomes high-risk under Article 6 is itself treated as the provider and assumes the Article 16 obligations, with the initial provider owing cooperation, information and technical access under Article 25(2). The schools deploying it carry Article 26 duties: use per the instructions, human oversight by competent, trained natural persons with the necessary authority and support, monitoring with notification of the provider and market surveillance authority plus suspension where a risk arises, and retention of automatically generated logs under their control for at least six months.

Before the operator places the system on the market, Article 23(1) requires the operator to satisfy yourself that it conforms to the Regulation by verifying four things: (a) that the provider has carried out the relevant conformity assessment procedure referred to in Article 43; (b) that the provider has drawn up the technical documentation in accordance with Article 11 and Annex IV; (c) that the system bears the required CE marking and is accompanied by the EU declaration of conformity referred to in Article 47 and by the instructions for use; and (d) that the provider has appointed an authorised representative in accordance with Article 22(1), that duty bites where the provider is established in a third country, which must appoint, by written mandate, a representative established in the Union prior to making the system available on the Union market, so the operator's check is that a valid mandate exists covering the tasks in Article 22(3). The verification is not complete at the checklist stage. Under Article 23(2), where you have sufficient reason to consider that the system is not in conformity, or is falsified, or is accompanied by falsified documentation, the operator must not place it on the market until it has been brought into conformity; and where the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), the operator must inform the provider, the authorised representative and the market surveillance authorities. In connection with placing it on the market the operator must also indicate the operator's name, registered trade name or registered trade mark, and the address at which the operator can be contacted on the high-risk AI system and on its packaging or accompanying documentation, where applicable (Article 23(3)), and ensure that, while the system is under the operator's responsibility, storage or transport conditions do not jeopardise its compliance with the Section 2 requirements (Article 23(4)). Thereafter the operator must keep, for 10 years after the system is placed on the market or put into service, a copy of the notified body certificate where applicable, of the instructions for use and of the EU declaration of conformity (Article 23(5)), supply competent authorities on reasoned request with all necessary information and documentation in a language easily understood by them and ensure the technical documentation can be made available to them (Article 23(6)), and cooperate with those authorities in any action concerning the system, in particular to reduce and mitigate its risks (Article 23(7)).

No. As a deployer the operator is not required to carry out a conformity assessment; that duty falls on the provider. The operator's housing-benefit eligibility system is high-risk under Article 6(2) because it is an AI system used by a public authority to evaluate the eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, and to grant, reduce, revoke or reclaim such benefits (Annex III, point 5(a)). For high-risk systems falling under points 2 to 8 of Annex III, Article 43(2) requires the provider to follow the conformity assessment procedure based on internal control set out in Annex VI, which does not provide for notified-body involvement; under Annex VI the provider verifies that the quality management system complies with Article 17, examines the technical documentation against the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements, and verifies that the design and development process and post-market monitoring under Article 72 are consistent with that documentation. The notified-body route in Annex VII is reserved for Annex III point 1 biometric systems where harmonised standards or common specifications have not been applied (Article 43(1)). The operator's practical duty is therefore to verify, before putting the system into service, that the provider has completed that assessment, i.e. that the system bears the CE marking, is accompanied by the EU declaration of conformity and the Article 13 instructions for use. What the operator must do before deployment is a fundamental rights impact assessment. Article 27(1) requires deployers that are bodies governed by public law, which a municipal authority is, to perform a FRIA before first use of an Article 6(2) high-risk system, covering the processes in which the system will be used in line with its intended purpose, the period and frequency of intended use, the categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected, the specific risks of harm to them, the human oversight measures to be implemented, and the measures to be taken if those risks materialise, including internal governance and complaint mechanisms. The Article 27(1) carve-out for systems intended for the Annex III point 2 critical-infrastructure area does not apply to the operator. Alongside the FRIA, Article 26 requires the operator to use the system in accordance with the instructions for use, to assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority (with the Article 14(4) capabilities enabling them to understand the system's capabilities and limitations, remain aware of automation bias, correctly interpret the output, decide not to use or to disregard, override or reverse it, and intervene or stop the system), to monitor operation, and to retain the automatically generated logs under the operator's control for at least six months (Article 26(6)). Because the system makes or assists in making decisions about natural persons, Article 26(11) obliges the operator to inform the affected applicants that they are subject to the use of a high-risk AI system. Article 4 additionally requires the operator to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among the operator's staff and others operating the system on the operator's behalf. One qualification: if you substantially modify the system within the meaning of Article 3(23), a new conformity assessment is required under Article 43(4), regardless of whether the modified system continues to be used by you as current deployer; pre-determined changes documented by the provider at the initial conformity assessment do not constitute a substantial modification.

Article 10 requires the operator to run the operator's training, validation and testing data sets through a documented data-governance regime, and, where the system is not trained on data, to apply that regime to the testing data sets only (Article 10(1) and 10(6)). Concretely, the governance and management practices must be appropriate to the intended purpose and must cover each of the following: the relevant design choices; the data collection processes and the origin of the data, including, for personal data, the original purpose of collection; the relevant data-preparation processing operations such as annotation, labelling, cleaning, updating, enrichment and aggregation; the formulation of assumptions, in particular about what the data are supposed to measure and represent; an assessment of the availability, quantity and suitability of the data sets needed; examination in view of possible biases likely to affect health and safety, to have a negative impact on fundamental rights, or to lead to discrimination, in particular where data outputs influence inputs for future operations; appropriate measures to detect, prevent and mitigate the biases so identified; and identification of relevant data gaps or shortcomings that prevent compliance, together with how they can be addressed (Article 10(2)(a), (h)). On quality, the data sets must be relevant, sufficiently representative and, to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose, with appropriate statistical properties including, where applicable, as regards the persons or groups of persons in relation to whom the system is intended to be used; these characteristics may be satisfied at the level of an individual data set or of a combination of data sets (Article 10(3)). The data sets must also reflect, to the extent required by the intended purpose, the characteristics or elements particular to the specific geographical, contextual, behavioural or functional setting of intended use (Article 10(4)). Where bias detection and correction requires special categories of personal data (the GDPR Article 9 categories), you may process them only to the extent strictly necessary and only under the cumulative conditions of Article 10(5): the objective cannot be effectively achieved by processing other data, including synthetic or anonymised data; the data are subject to technical limitations on re-use and to state-of-the-art security and privacy-preserving measures, including pseudonymisation; the data are secured, protected and subject to suitable safeguards, including strict controls and documentation of access, so that only authorised persons with appropriate confidentiality duties can access them; the data are not transmitted, transferred or otherwise accessed by other parties; the data are deleted once the bias has been corrected or the personal data reach the end of their retention period, whichever comes first; and the records of processing activities include the reasons why processing those categories was strictly necessary to detect and correct bias and why that objective could not be achieved by processing other data. Operationally, these steps must be embedded as written systems and procedures for data management, acquisition, collection, analysis, labelling, storage, filtration, mining, aggregation and retention performed before and for the purpose of placing on the market or putting into service, within the quality management system (Article 17(1)(f)), and the residual data-related risks, including bias-driven risks to fundamental rights, must be carried through the iterative risk-management process and addressed by targeted risk-management measures (Article 9(2)(a) and (d)).

Treat this as a serious incident involving a high-risk AI system and act on the deployer's immediate duties now, in parallel: suspend, notify, preserve logs. Emergency healthcare patient triage systems are expressly listed in Annex III, point 5, so the system is high-risk under Article 6(2) (the Article 6(3) derogation is unavailable because triage is neither a narrow procedural nor a preparatory task and it determines the outcome for the patient). Harm to a patient is a "serious incident" within Article 3, point 49, since it involves serious harm to a person's health. As deployer, Article 26(5) requires the operator to monitor operation on the basis of the instructions for use and, where you have reason to consider that use in accordance with those instructions may nevertheless present a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), to inform the provider or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authority without undue delay and to suspend use of the system. Where a serious incident has been identified, the operator must immediately inform first the provider, and then the importer or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authority. Article 26(1) means the operator should also verify whether the mis-triage arose from use outside the instructions for use, since that determines whether the corrective action is organisational (retraining oversight staff, restoring the human-oversight step) or a product-side defect for the provider to address. Under Article 26(6) the automatically generated logs, to the extent under the operator's control, must be retained for a period appropriate to the intended purpose and in any event at least six months, preserve the full log record for the incident window now, before any rotation or retention policy deletes it, as it is the evidentiary basis for both the provider's and the authority's assessment. On the provider side, Article 73 requires reporting of the serious incident to the market surveillance authority of the Member State where the incident occurred, immediately upon establishing a causal link or a reasonably likely causal link between the AI system and the incident, and in any event not later than 15 days after awareness; not later than 10 days after the date of awareness in the event of death; and immediately, and not later than 2 days, for a widespread infringement or a serious and irreversible disruption of critical infrastructure. An initial incomplete report may be filed and completed subsequently. Importantly, if the triage system is itself a medical device or a safety component of one under Regulation (EU) 2017/745 or (EU) 2017/746, Article 73 reporting is narrowed to incidents constituting an infringement of Union law protecting fundamental rights, notified to the national competent authority designated for that purpose; death or serious deterioration of health routes instead through MDR vigilance, and the Article 73(2) to (4) clocks apply only to the residual AI Act track. Finally, the harmed patient has a right under Article 86(1) to obtain from you a clear and meaningful explanation of the role the system played in the triage decision and the main elements of the decision taken, unless an exception or restriction follows from Union or national law (Article 86(2)) or the right is already provided for under other Union law (Article 86(3)). Expect the market surveillance authority to open an Article 79 evaluation and to be able to require withdrawal, recall or restriction of the system.

Article 86 grants that right. Because an AI system used to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score is a listed high-risk use-case under Annex III, point 5(b) (the only carve-out there being systems used to detect financial fraud), the operator's loan-eligibility system falls within Annex III and outside the Annex III, point 2 critical-infrastructure exclusion that Article 86 makes. An applicant denied credit is therefore an affected person subject to a decision taken by you as deployer on the basis of the output of that high-risk system, and the denial produces legal effects or similarly significantly adversely affects their fundamental rights; on that basis the applicant has the right to obtain from you a clear and meaningful explanation of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and of the main elements of the decision taken. The right is owed by the deployer, not the provider, and it applies without prejudice to, and does not replace, the rights in Article 22 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679; nor does it displace the separate duty under Article 26(11) to inform the natural person, before or at the point of use, that they are subject to the use of the high-risk AI system. Note that the Article 86 explanation right is triggered only where the decision rests on the system's output and has such legal or similarly significant adverse effect, and it does not extend to Annex III, point 2 systems.

Adding an AI reply-suggestion feature does not make the operator's system high-risk, but it does take it out of the wholly unregulated minimal-risk category and into the Article 50 transparency tier. On classification, neither the spam filter nor the reply generator is a safety component of, or itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I subject to third-party conformity assessment, so the Article 6(1) route is not engaged. Nor does sorting junk mail or drafting canned business correspondence fall within any lettered use-case under the eight Annex III areas (biometrics; critical infrastructure; education and vocational training; employment, workers' management and access to self-employment; access to and enjoyment of essential private and public services; law enforcement; migration, asylum and border control management; administration of justice and democratic processes), so Article 6(2) is not engaged either. Because the system is not an Annex III system at all, you do not need the documented Article 6(4) self-assessment, that derogation exercise only arises for systems that are within Annex III. Annex III can be widened only by Commission delegated act under Article 7(1), which requires cumulatively that the systems are used in an area already listed (Article 7(1)(a)) and pose an equivalent or greater risk than the systems already listed (Article 7(1)(b)), adopted under Article 97; no such act reclassifies this product today. What does change is transparency. The reply generator produces synthetic text, so as provider the operator must mark the outputs in a machine-readable format and make them detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, using solutions that are effective, interoperable, robust and reliable (Article 50(2)). That duty is disapplied only where the AI performs an assistive standard editing function that does not substantially alter the input data provided by the deployer or its semantics, or where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, a pure autocomplete-style tidy-up of a human-written draft may fall in the first carve-out, but generating a whole reply does not. If the feature is ever exposed so that it converses directly with the recipient rather than proposing text to the operator's business customer's staff, Article 50(1) additionally requires that the natural person be informed they are interacting with an AI system. The Article 50(4) deepfake and public-interest-text duties are deployer duties and are not triggered by ordinary business correspondence; in any event that text duty does not apply where the content has undergone human review or editorial control and a person holds editorial responsibility for publishing it. None of the Article 5 prohibited practices are engaged on these facts, and the Chapter III provider obligations in Articles 16 to 19 remain inapplicable unless the intended purpose is later modified so the system becomes high-risk under Article 6.

Yes, inferring users' religious or philosophical beliefs and political opinions from biometric data is a prohibited AI practice, not merely a high-risk system. Article 5(1)(g) prohibits the placing on the market, the putting into service for this specific purpose, or the use of biometric categorisation systems that categorise individually natural persons based on their biometric data to deduce or infer their race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation. The operator's ad-targeting use case falls squarely within two of those listed attributes, and commercial audience segmentation is exactly the "use" the provision reaches; the prohibition is attribute-based and carries no legitimate-interest, consent or contractual justification. The only carve-outs in Article 5(1)(g) are that the prohibition does not cover the labelling or filtering of lawfully acquired biometric datasets, such as images, based on biometric data, nor the categorising of biometric data in the area of law enforcement. Neither is available to a commercial advertising deployer: labelling or filtering a lawfully acquired dataset is a dataset-management operation, not the individual categorisation of natural persons to deduce sensitive attributes, and the operator is not a law-enforcement actor. Because the practice is prohibited, the high-risk analysis is displaced rather than alternative. Annex III, point 1 is expressly conditioned on biometric uses "in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law", and Annex III, point 1(b) covers AI systems intended to be used for biometric categorisation according to sensitive or protected attributes based on the inference of those attributes. A system that infers religion or political opinion from biometric data cannot be brought into compliance by treating it as an Article 6(2) high-risk system and discharging the Chapter III duties (Article 10 data governance, Article 13 instructions for use, Article 15 accuracy and robustness, Article 16 provider duties, Article 26 deployer duties, Article 49 registration); those obligations do not license an Article 5 practice, and the Article 6(3) derogation is likewise unavailable since profiling of natural persons always remains high-risk. Two boundary points define what you may still do. First, grouping users by stated interests, self-declared, non-biometric input, is outside Article 5(1)(g) entirely, since the prohibition is triggered by categorisation "based on their biometric data"; it is the biometric inference layer, not the interest segmentation, that is unlawful. Second, if the system performs biometric categorisation only on attributes that are not among the listed sensitive ones, it escapes Article 5(1)(g) but is high-risk under Annex III, point 1(b) where those attributes are otherwise protected, and the deployer must in any event inform the natural persons exposed to it of its operation under Article 50(3), an obligation preserved alongside the Article 13 transparency chain by Article 26(11). The compliant course is to remove the biometric inference of religious or philosophical beliefs and political opinions from the system's intended purpose and from its actual operation.

Under the AI Act you do not file with a sectoral regulator: registration is made in the EU database for high-risk AI systems set up and managed by the Commission, which is the controller of that database (Article 71(1) and (6)). The provider or, where applicable, its authorised representative must register itself and the system there before the system is placed on the market or put into service (Article 49(1)), and this is the registration obligation carried in the provider-obligations list at Article 16(1)(i); the provider or authorised representative enters the Annex VIII Section A and B data (Article 71(2)). The same EU-database registration applies where you have concluded under Article 6(3) that an Annex III system is not high-risk, that self-assessment must be documented before placing on the market and the system still registered under Article 49(2) (Article 6(4)). Where the deployer is a public authority, Union institution, body, office or agency, or a person acting on its behalf, it registers itself, selects the system and registers its use in the same database, entering the Annex VIII Section C data (Articles 49(3) and 71(3)). Two carve-outs matter. First, for Annex III point 2 systems (critical infrastructure) there is no EU-database entry at all: those are registered at national level (Article 49(5)), and the Article 49(1), (3) duties expressly exclude them. Second, for systems under Annex III points 1, 6 and 7 (biometrics, and law enforcement, migration, asylum and border-control management), registration under Article 49(1), (2) and (3) goes into a secure non-public section of the EU database and is limited to Annex VIII Section A points 1 to 10 excluding points 6, 8 and 9; Annex VIII Section B points 1 to 5 and points 8 and 9; Annex VIII Section C points 1 to 3; and Annex IX points 1, 2, 3 and 5, accessible only to the Commission and the national authorities referred to in Article 74(8) (Article 49(4)). All other Article 49 registrations are publicly accessible in machine-readable, easily navigable form (Article 71(4)). If the provider is established in a third country, an authorised representative established in the Union must be appointed by written mandate before the system is made available on the Union market, and the mandate must empower it to comply with the Article 49(1) registration obligations or, where the provider registers itself, to ensure that the Annex VIII Section A point 3 information is correct (Articles 22(1) and 22(3)(e)). Separately from registration, national competent authorities remain the addressees for the documentation the operator must hold: the EU declaration of conformity kept at their disposal for 10 years (Article 47(1)), the Annex IV technical documentation (Article 11(1)), and the Article 6(4) non-high-risk assessment on request. Failure to comply with the Article 16 provider obligations, including registration, is subject to fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, with the lower of the two ceilings applying to SMEs and start-ups (Article 99(4)(a) and (6)).The answer is complete as written; no tail remains beyond the final sentence's punctuation.

No, an Article 35 GDPR data protection impact assessment does not discharge the AI Act obligation; where Article 27(1) applies the operator must still perform a fundamental rights impact assessment, and Article 27(4) provides only that where any of the Article 27 obligations are already met through the DPIA conducted under Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (or Article 27 of Directive (EU) 2016/680), the FRIA complements that assessment. "Complement" means no duplication of elements already properly covered, but the FRIA remains the governing instrument and its uncovered elements, its notification step and its update duty must still be satisfied. The duty bites only if the operator's organisation is within Article 27(1)'s actor and use scope: deployers that are bodies governed by public law or private entities providing public services, and deployers of the Annex III point 5(b) creditworthiness and credit-scoring systems and the Annex III point 5(c) risk assessment and pricing systems in life and health insurance, deploying a high-risk AI system referred to in Article 6(2), expressly excluding systems intended to be used in the Annex III point 2 critical-infrastructure area (safety components in the management and operation of critical digital infrastructure, road traffic, or the supply of water, gas, heating or electricity). Where it applies, the assessment must cover the six limbs of Article 27(1): (a) a description of the deployer's processes in which the system will be used in line with its intended purpose; (b) the period of time within which, and the frequency with which, the system is intended to be used; (c) the categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected in the specific context; (d) the specific risks of harm likely to have an impact on those categories; (e) a description of the implementation of human oversight measures, according to the instructions for use; and (f) the measures to be taken in the case of the materialisation of those risks, including arrangements for internal governance and complaint mechanisms. A typical GDPR DPIA will not, on its face, contain (b), (e) or (f) in these terms, which is where the gap usually sits. Three further AI Act steps have no GDPR analogue. Under Article 27(2) the obligation attaches to the first use of the high-risk AI system; in similar cases the deployer may rely on previously conducted fundamental rights impact assessments or on existing impact assessments carried out by the provider, and must take the necessary steps to update the information if any Article 27(1) element has changed or is no longer up to date. Under Article 27(3) the deployer must, once the assessment is performed, notify the market surveillance authority of its results, submitting the filled-out template as part of the notification, with a possible exemption from that notification duty in the case referred to in Article 46(1). Under Article 27(5) the AI Office is to develop a questionnaire template, including through an automated tool, to facilitate simplified compliance, so the practical route is to map the operator's DPO's existing DPIA onto the Article 27(1) limbs, fill the residual limbs, and notify.

The AI Act's window is three months. Under Article 79(8), where no objection is raised within three months of receipt of the notification referred to in Article 79(5), either by a market surveillance authority of another Member State or by the Commission, the provisional measure taken by the initiating authority is deemed justified. That three-month period is reduced to 30 days where the non-compliance concerns the prohibited AI practices referred to in Article 5. Expiry of the window is without prejudice to the procedural rights of the operator concerned under Article 18 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020. The surrounding steps set the rest of the timing. The period for the operator to take corrective action is not a fixed figure in the Regulation: under Article 79(2) the market surveillance authority, having evaluated the system against all requirements and obligations of the Regulation, fixes the period itself, and the operator must extend the corrective action to all AI systems concerned that it has made available on the Union market (Article 79(4)). Where non-compliance is not restricted to national territory, the authority informs the Commission and the other Member States "without undue delay" (Article 79(3)). If adequate corrective action is not taken within the period set under Article 79(2), the authority takes provisional measures, prohibition or restriction of making available or putting into service, withdrawal, or recall, and notifies the Commission and the other Member States without undue delay (Article 79(5)); that notification must identify the non-compliant system, its origin and supply chain, the nature of the alleged non-compliance and the risk, the nature and duration of the national measures, and the operator's arguments, indicating whether the non-compliance stems from Article 5 prohibited practices, failure of a high-risk system to meet Chapter III, Section 2 requirements, shortcomings in the harmonised standards or common specifications referred to in Articles 40 and 41, or non-compliance with Article 50 (Article 79(6)). Other market surveillance authorities must, also without undue delay, inform the Commission and the other Member States of measures adopted, of additional information, and of any objections to the notified national measure (Article 79(7)), and restrictive measures such as withdrawal must be taken without undue delay (Article 79(9)).

Fine-tuning the vendor's system on the operator's five-year hiring dataset is a substantial modification within Article 25(1)(b), so you assume the full provider obligations for that system; Vendor X ceases to be its provider and must cooperate with you, supplying the necessary information, reasonably expected technical access and other assistance, in particular for the conformity assessment, subject only to intellectual property, confidential business information and trade-secret protection (Article 25(2) and (5)). The hand-over carve-out in Article 25(2) for initial providers who excluded conversion into a high-risk system does not help here, because the system is already high-risk: CV screening for shortlisting falls within Annex III, point 4, and thus within Article 6(2). The Article 6(3) derogation is unavailable, shortlisting is not a narrow procedural task, an improvement of a completed human activity, pattern/deviation detection, or a merely preparatory task, it materially influences the hiring outcome, and any system performing profiling of natural persons is always high-risk. As provider the operator must now satisfy the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements and the Article 16 duties. Establish, implement, document and maintain an iterative lifecycle risk-management system identifying foreseeable risks to health, safety and fundamental rights in intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse, evaluating post-market data, adopting targeted mitigation, and testing against pre-defined metrics (Article 9(1), (6)). The operator's own hiring data now makes you responsible for data governance: design choices, provenance and collection, preparation, assumptions, assessment of availability and quantity, examination for biases likely to lead to prohibited discrimination, acute where five years of past decisions encode past preferences, measures to detect, prevent and mitigate them, and identification of data gaps, with datasets relevant, sufficiently representative, error-free and complete and reflecting the geographic, contextual and behavioural setting of use (Article 10(2), (4)); special-category data may be processed only where strictly necessary for bias detection and correction under the safeguards in Article 10(5). Draw up Annex IV technical documentation before placing on the market or putting into service and keep it up to date (Article 11(1)); ensure automatic logging retained at least six months (Articles 12 and 16(1)(e)). Design for transparency and supply instructions for use giving the operator's identity and contact details, intended purpose, declared accuracy metrics, robustness and cybersecurity levels, foreseeable risk circumstances, explanation capabilities, performance on specific groups, input-data specifications, output-interpretation guidance, pre-determined changes, human-oversight measures, computational and hardware resources, and the mechanism for collecting, storing and interpreting logs (Articles 13(1), (3) and 15(3)). Build in effective human oversight enabling capability awareness, automation-bias vigilance, output interpretation, disregard or override and intervention (Article 14(1), (5)), and appropriate accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, including feedback-loop mitigation if it keeps learning (Article 15(1), (5)). Operationally, run a documented quality-management system (Article 17), complete the Annex VI internal-control conformity assessment (Article 43), draw up the signed, dated, machine-readable EU declaration of conformity with the Annex V content (Article 47), affix CE marking (Article 48), register yourself and the system in the EU database before placing it on the market or putting it into service (Article 49), and operate a post-market monitoring plan and system feeding back into risk management with corrective-action and incident-reporting workflows (Articles 72 and 17). Article 16 additionally requires the operator's name and address on the system, retention of documentation and logs, corrective action and demonstration of conformity on request. The operator's deployer duties persist alongside these: use per the instructions, assign oversight to competent, trained natural persons with the necessary authority and support, monitor operation, keep the logs under the operator's control for at least six months, inform affected workers' representatives and workers before putting the system into service, and inform candidates that they are subject to its use (Article 26). A fundamental-rights impact assessment under Article 27 is required only if the operator is a body governed by public law or a private entity providing public services; an ordinary private employer is not caught. Article 50(1) disclosure applies only where the system interacts directly with candidates. Finally, ensure AI literacy among staff operating the system (Article 4).

An enterprise that develops a GPT‑style system and puts it into service under its own name for its own internal HR use is simultaneously the provider (it is the entity that develops the system and puts it into service under its own name, including for its own use) and the deployer (it uses the system under its own authority), and it carries the two sets of obligations cumulatively. The same result follows under Article 25 if the model is third‑party in origin: a deployer becomes a provider and assumes all provider obligations where it puts its own name or trademark on a high‑risk system, makes a substantial modification to it, or modifies its intended purpose so that it becomes high‑risk. That dual status matters because AI systems intended to be used for recruitment or selection, for decisions on promotion, termination, task allocation, or for monitoring and evaluating performance and behaviour of persons in work‑related relationships fall within Annex III, point 4, and are therefore high‑risk. As provider the operator must satisfy Chapter III, Section 2 in full: a documented, iterative risk‑management system over the lifecycle, with consideration of adverse impact on persons under 18 and other vulnerable groups and the option to integrate it into existing internal risk‑management procedures required by other Union law (Article 9(1), (9), (10)); data‑governance and quality criteria for training, validation and testing data sets, which must be relevant, sufficiently representative and to the best extent possible free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose (Article 10(1), (3)); technical documentation per Annex IV drawn up before the system is put into service and kept up to date (Article 11(1)); automatic logging (Article 12(1), (2)); transparency and instructions for use covering intended purpose, accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity metrics, foreseeable risks including under reasonably foreseeable misuse, explanation capabilities, performance for specific persons or groups, input‑data specifications and output‑interpretation information (Article 13(3)(b)(i), (vii)); human‑oversight design (Article 14); accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity (Article 15); a quality management system (Article 17); conformity assessment by the internal‑control route under Annex VI (Article 43); a signed EU declaration of conformity with the Annex V content (Article 47); CE marking (Article 48); registration of yourself and the system in the EU database before putting it into service (Article 49); post‑market monitoring (Article 72); and serious‑incident reporting on the tiered deadlines (Article 73). As deployer the operator must additionally use the system in accordance with the instructions for use (Article 26(1)), assign human oversight to competent, trained natural persons with the necessary authority and support (Article 26(2)), ensure input data is relevant and sufficiently representative (Article 26(4)), monitor operation and suspend use and inform the provider and market surveillance authority where risks arise (Article 26(5)), retain the automatically generated logs under the operator's control for at least six months (Article 26(6)), and, as an employer deploying at the workplace, inform workers' representatives and the affected workers before putting the system into service (Article 26(7)); the operator must also inform natural persons that they are subject to its use where it makes or assists decisions about them (Article 26(11)) and cooperate with the competent authorities (Article 26(12)). These duties are without prejudice to other deployer obligations under Union or national law and to the operator's freedom to organise the operator's own resources for implementing the oversight measures the provider indicates (Article 26(3)). The fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27 does not attach to you on these facts: that duty is confined to deployers that are bodies governed by public law or private entities providing public services, and to deployers of the Annex III, point 5(b) and (c) creditworthiness and life/health‑insurance systems, an ordinary private employer deploying an Annex III, point 4 HR system is outside it, though if you were within scope the assessment would have to be done before first use, could rely on prior or provider assessments in similar cases, would have to be updated when elements change, and would have to be notified to the market surveillance authority on the AI Office template (Article 27(2), (3), (5)). Two further points apply in both capacities. Article 4 requires the operator to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among staff and others operating the system on the operator's behalf, as provider and as deployer. Article 50 adds transparency duties: as provider the operator must ensure the system discloses to candidates and employees that they are interacting with an AI system (Article 50(1)) and mark synthetic audio, image, video or text outputs in a machine‑readable, detectable format using effective, interoperable, robust and reliable solutions, excepted where the system performs an assistive function for standard editing, does not substantially alter the input data or its semantics, or is authorised by law for the detection, prevention, investigation or prosecution of criminal offences (Article 50(2)); these transparency duties do not affect the Chapter III requirements (Article 50(6)). Finally, screen the HR use case against Article 5, which prohibits inter alia subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques causing significant harm and exploitation of vulnerabilities by age, disability or socio‑economic situation, and which bars inferring emotions in the workplace outside medical or safety purposes.

Putting the operator's own name or trademark on the system makes you its provider. Article 25(1)(a) provides that any distributor, importer, deployer or other third party shall be considered a provider of a high-risk AI system and becomes subject to the provider obligations under Article 16 where they put their name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service, without prejudice to contractual arrangements stipulating that the obligations are otherwise allocated. The same consequence follows under Article 25(1)(b) where they make a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service in such a way that it remains high-risk pursuant to Article 6, and under Article 25(1)(c) where they modify the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, not classified as high-risk so that it becomes high-risk. Rebranding alone is enough; no technical change is needed. Under Article 25(2), the original provider ceases to be the provider of that specific system, but must cooperate closely, make available the necessary information and provide the technical access and other assistance reasonably expected, so the operator should secure the Annex IV documentation, datasets evidence and test records contractually before the rebrand. As provider the operator must then, in the operator's own name, operate the risk management system (Article 9), meet the data-governance requirements (Article 10), hold and keep up to date the technical documentation drawn up before placing on the market (Article 11(1)), ensure automatic logging (Article 12), supply instructions for use identifying you as provider (Article 13), build in human-oversight measures (Article 14(3)(a) and (b)), meet accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity requirements (Article 15), run a quality management system (Article 17), complete conformity assessment (Article 43), draw up the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47), affix the CE marking (Article 48), register yourself and the system in the EU database before placing it on the market (Article 49(1)), and operate post-market monitoring (Article 72) and serious-incident reporting (Article 73). Article 4 AI literacy and, where the system interacts with natural persons or generates synthetic content, the provider duties in Article 50(1) and (2) also apply to the operator, subject to the Article 50(1) carve-outs where the AI nature is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person or where the system is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, unless available for the public to report an offence; the Article 5 prohibitions apply regardless. If the system is not high-risk under Article 6 and you do not alter its intended purpose, Article 25(1) is not triggered by the rebrand, though Article 49(2) registration applies where you conclude a system is not high-risk under Article 6(3).

No. Cumulative training compute of exactly 1×10²⁵ FLOPs does not, by itself, change the operator's classification: Article 51(2) presumes high-impact capabilities only when the cumulative amount of computation used for training, measured in floating-point operations, is greater than 10²⁵, so a model sitting precisely at the threshold is not caught by the presumption, and the Commission's 18 July 2025 GPAI Guidelines are interpretive guidance that cannot alter that statutory figure, only a delegated act under Article 51(3), adopted in accordance with Article 97, may amend the thresholds in Article 51(1) and (2). Two qualifications follow from Article 51(1). First, the presumption in paragraph 2 is not the only route into systemic risk: under Article 51(1)(a) a model is classified as having systemic risk where it has high impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks, independently of the compute figure; and under Article 51(1)(b) the Commission may so classify it by decision, acting ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel, where the model has capabilities or an impact equivalent to point (a), having regard to the Annex XIII criteria (parameter count, dataset quality and size, training compute, input and output modalities, benchmarks and capability evaluations, reach in terms of business users and EU registered end-users, and number of registered users). Second, compute is cumulative, so any further training that takes the total above 10²⁵ FLOPs does trigger the paragraph 2 presumption; the operator's measurement and documentation of that figure feeds Annex XI, and the Commission may under Article 53(5) adopt delegated acts detailing measurement and calculation methodologies for comparable and verifiable documentation. Until the threshold is exceeded or a decision under Article 51(1)(b) is taken, the operator's obligations remain those in Article 53(1): drawing up and keeping up to date the Annex XI technical documentation of the model, including its training and testing process and evaluation results, for provision on request to the AI Office and national competent authorities (point (a)); drawing up, keeping up to date and making available to downstream providers integrating the model the information and documentation that enables them to understand the model's capabilities and limitations and meet their own obligations, containing at least the Annex XII elements (point (b)); putting in place a copyright policy, in particular to identify and comply with a rights reservation expressed under Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790, through state-of-the-art technologies (point (c)); and publishing a sufficiently detailed summary of the training content according to the AI Office template (point (d)). If the model is released under a free and open-source licence permitting access, use, modification and distribution with publicly available parameters, weights, architecture information and usage information, Article 53(2) disapplies points (a) and (b) only, but that exception expressly falls away for general-purpose AI models with systemic risk. Should the cumulative figure later exceed 10²⁵ FLOPs, Article 55(1) adds, on top of Articles 53 and 54: (a) model evaluation under standardised protocols and tools reflecting the state of the art, including conducting and documenting adversarial testing to identify and mitigate systemic risks; (b) assessing and mitigating possible Union-level systemic risks, including their sources, stemming from development, placing on the market or use of the model; (c) keeping track of, documenting and reporting without undue delay to the AI Office and, as appropriate, to national competent authorities relevant information on serious incidents and possible corrective measures; and (d) ensuring an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure. Compliance may be demonstrated through codes of practice under Article 56 until a harmonised standard is published, per Articles 53(4) and 55(2), with information so obtained protected under Article 78.

No, a fine-tune at 3.3×10²⁴ FLOPs does not, of itself, make you a provider under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as adopted. The "one third of the original training compute" figure is not a threshold in the adopted text; it comes from Commission guidance on downstream modifiers, and guidance does not independently create statutory duties or provider status. Compute appears in the Regulation only as one of the criteria for designating a general-purpose AI model as presenting systemic risk (Annex XIII, alongside parameter count, dataset quality and size, modalities, benchmarks and capability evaluations, and reach measured in business users and registered EU end-users), and Recital 112 explains only that a model meeting the applicable high-impact-capabilities threshold is presumed to be a model with systemic risk, that is a classification question about the model, not a rule that transfers provider status to whoever fine-tuned it. What actually determines whether the operator becomes a provider is Article 25(1): a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party is treated as the provider of a high-risk AI system, and assumes the Article 16 provider obligations, where (a) it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service, without prejudice to contractual arrangements allocating the obligations otherwise; (b) it makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service such that it remains high-risk under Article 6; or (c) it modifies the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, not classified as high-risk and already placed on the market or put into service, in such a way that it becomes high-risk under Article 6. Each limb turns on branding, substantial modification or change of intended purpose, none on a compute ratio. So the relevant questions for the operator's fine-tune are whether you release it under the operator's own name or trademark, whether the modification is substantial to a system that stays high-risk, or whether you have redirected the intended purpose into a high-risk use. If one of those circumstances is met, the consequences follow from the same Article: the initial provider ceases to be the provider of that specific system, must cooperate closely with you and make available the necessary information, reasonably expected technical access and other assistance, in particular as regards conformity assessment, except where that initial provider has clearly specified that its system is not to be changed into a high-risk AI system, in which case the hand-over duty does not apply (Article 25(2)); and where you instead supply a model, tools, services, components or processes integrated into someone else's high-risk system, you and that provider must specify the necessary information, capabilities, technical access and assistance by written agreement, save for third parties making tools, services, processes or components other than general-purpose AI models publicly available under a free and open-source licence (Article 25(4)). All of this operates without prejudice to intellectual property rights, confidential business information and trade secrets (Article 25(5)). Independently of Article 25, the AI-literacy duty in Article 4 and the transparency duties in Article 50 bind you in whatever capacity, provider or deployer, you in fact occupy.

Yes, at 2×10²⁵ FLOPs the open-source carve-out is lost and the full documentation obligations apply. Cumulative training compute greater than 10²⁵ floating point operations triggers the presumption of high-impact capabilities under Article 51(2), which classifies the model as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk under Article 51(1)(a). Article 53(2) disapplies the Article 53(1)(a) and (b) obligations for models released under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution with publicly available parameters, weights, architecture information and model usage information, but its second sentence states that this exception shall not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk. An Apache 2.0 release of open weights on HuggingFace would otherwise satisfy the licence and publicity conditions, yet that is irrelevant once the compute threshold is crossed: the licence route cannot displace a systemic-risk classification. Consequently the operator must, under Article 53(1)(a), draw up and keep up to date technical documentation of the model including its training and testing process and evaluation results, containing at a minimum the Annex XI information, for provision on request to the AI Office and national competent authorities; and, under Article 53(1)(b), draw up, keep up to date and make available to providers of AI systems intending to integrate the model information and documentation that enables them to understand the model's capabilities and limitations and to comply with their own obligations and that contains at a minimum the Annex XII elements, without prejudice to intellectual property rights and confidential business information or trade secrets. The Article 53(1)(c) copyright policy, including identifying and complying with rights reservations expressed under Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790 through state-of-the-art technologies, and the Article 53(1)(d) publicly available sufficiently detailed training-content summary per the AI Office template applied in any event, open-source or not, since Article 53(2) never covered them. The classification also adds the Article 55(1) obligations on top of Article 53: (a) model evaluation under standardised state-of-the-art protocols and tools, including conducting and documenting adversarial testing to identify and mitigate systemic risks; (b) assessment and mitigation of possible Union-level systemic risks, including their sources, stemming from development, placing on the market or use; (c) tracking, documenting and reporting without undue delay to the AI Office and, as appropriate, national competent authorities, relevant information on serious incidents and possible corrective measures; and (d) an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure. Until a harmonised standard is published you may rely on Article 56 codes of practice to demonstrate compliance with both Article 53(1) and Article 55(1), per Articles 53(4) and 55(2); otherwise the operator must demonstrate alternative adequate means of compliance for Commission assessment. Information obtained under these Articles, including trade secrets, is handled under the Article 78 confidentiality regime by virtue of Articles 53(7) and 55(3). The presumption in Article 51(2) is rebuttable only in the sense that classification rests on high-impact capabilities under Article 51(1)(a); absent a successful demonstration to the Commission that the model does not have such capabilities notwithstanding the compute figure, 2×10²⁵ FLOPs leaves you outside Article 53(2) entirely.

Neither provision displaces the other: Article 13 and Article 50(1) apply cumulatively to the same medical‑triage chatbot, because Article 50(6) expressly provides that paragraphs 1 to 4 of Article 50 "shall not affect the requirements and obligations set out in Chapter III", the high‑risk regime that contains and are without prejudice to other transparency obligations under Union or national law. There is therefore no lex specialis hierarchy to resolve; the two duties have different addressees and different beneficiaries and must both be satisfied. Article 13 is transparency toward the deployer: the provider must design the system so its operation is sufficiently transparent to enable the deployer to interpret its output and use it appropriately (Article 13(1)), accompany it with concise, complete, correct and clear instructions for use (Article 13(2)), and include in those instructions at least the provider's and authorised representative's identity and contact details; the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance, intended purpose, the tested level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity and circumstances affecting it, known or foreseeable circumstances that may lead to risks to health, safety or fundamental rights including under reasonably foreseeable misuse, output‑explanation capabilities, performance regarding specific persons or groups, input‑data specifications, and information enabling interpretation of the output; pre‑determined changes to the system and its performance; the human oversight measures under Article 14; the computational and hardware resources, expected lifetime and necessary maintenance and care measures including software updates; and, where relevant, the logging mechanisms allowing deployers to collect, store and interpret logs (Article 13(3)). Article 50(1) is transparency toward the patient: the provider must design and develop the chatbot so that the natural person is informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless that is obvious to a reasonably well‑informed, observant and circumspect person in the circumstances and context of use, and the duty does not apply to systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences (subject to safeguards for third‑party rights), unless the system is available for the public to report a criminal offence, a carve‑out with no realistic application to clinical triage. That disclosure must be given clearly and distinguishably at the latest at the time of the first interaction and must conform to applicable accessibility requirements (Article 50(5)).
