Practically, the "obvious" exception in Article 50(1) is the only point of interaction between the two regimes, and it cannot be satisfied by Article 13 compliance: information delivered in the instructions for use reaches the deploying health institution, not the triaged patient, so a provider cannot rely on deployer‑facing documentation to discharge the end‑user disclosure. Where the triage system is an Annex III high‑risk system that makes or assists in making decisions about natural persons, the deployer additionally owes the Article 26(11) duty to inform those persons that they are subject to its use, expressly "without prejudice to Article 50", confirming the additive rather than exclusive structure of these transparency duties.

No, priority access under Article 62(1)(a) does not carry over. That measure is addressed to Member States for the benefit of SMEs, including start-ups, having a registered office or a branch in the Union, and it attaches to the operator's status at the time you apply to the sandbox; it is not a vested or grandfathered entitlement that survives the operator's growth. At 250 employees and €60 million turnover you exceed the staff headcount ceiling (fewer than 250 persons) and the turnover ceiling (€50 million) of the SME definition on which the Regulation relies, so the Article 62(1)(a) priority ceases once that loss of SME status becomes definitive under that definition's own rule that the ceilings must be exceeded over two consecutive accounting periods. Losing the priority does not lose you the sandbox. Article 62(1)(a) only ranks access and expressly provides that priority access shall not preclude other SMEs that meet the eligibility conditions and selection criteria; correspondingly, Article 57 opens the national AI regulatory sandbox, which each Member State must ensure is operational by 2 August 2026, to providers and prospective providers generally, under a specific sandbox plan agreed with the competent authority (Article 57(1) and (5)). Whatever the operator's size, participation still turns on satisfying the sandbox's eligibility conditions and selection criteria, and retain the substantive benefits of participation: guidance, supervision and support in identifying and mitigating risks (Article 57(6)); written proof of activities successfully carried out and an exit report usable to demonstrate compliance in conformity assessment or market surveillance (Article 57(7)); and the protection in Article 57(12) whereby, while you remain liable for damage to third parties, no administrative fines are imposed for infringements of this Regulation where you observe the sandbox plan and terms and follow the competent authority's guidance in good faith. The other Article 62 accommodations follow the same logic. The SME-tailored awareness-raising and training activities (Article 62(1)(b)) and the facilitation of SME participation in standardisation (Article 62(1)(d)) are directed at SMEs, including start-ups, so they no longer target you; the dedicated communication channels under Article 62(1)(c) remain available to you as a deployer and as one of the "other innovators" addressed there, including as regards participation in sandboxes. The reduction of conformity assessment fees under Article 62(2) is conditioned on the specific interests and needs of SME providers and is set proportionately to size, market size and other relevant indicators, so at the operator's new scale the proportionality factors no longer support a reduction. The AI Office measures in Article 62(3), standardised templates, the single information platform, communication campaigns, and promotion of best practices in public procurement, are addressed to all operators and are unaffected by the operator's size.

Yes, an emotion recognition tool placed on the market for, or used to, infer the emotions of call‑centre agents is a prohibited practice, because a call centre is the agents' workplace and Article 5(1)(f) bans the placing on the market, the putting into service for this specific purpose, and the use of AI systems to infer emotions of a natural person in the area of the workplace. The prohibition bites on you as provider at the point of sale for that stated purpose, not only on the deploying call centre; the chapeau of Article 5(1) makes all three commercial acts equally prohibited, so a contractual disclaimer or a "wellbeing only" framing does not cure it. Article 5(1)(f) carries a single exhaustive carve‑out: systems intended to be put in place or into the market for medical or safety reasons. That exception is narrow and purpose‑bound, it covers therapeutic use or the detection of states relevant to the physical safety of persons, not productivity, quality‑assurance, coaching, churn‑prediction or staff‑wellbeing analytics, which is how stress scoring is normally sold to contact centres. Two further scope conditions can place a given product outside the prohibition entirely. First, the system must infer emotions or intentions on the basis of biometric data; a tool that classifies only the textual content of chat transcripts or ticket notes, without processing voice, face or other biometric signals, is not an emotion recognition system at all. Second, as Recital 18 explains, the notion covers emotions such as anger, satisfaction or embarrassment and does not extend to physical states such as pain or fatigue; if the product genuinely measures a physiological state rather than inferring an emotional one, and does so for accident prevention, it falls outside Article 5(1)(f), but marketing it as detecting "stress", frustration or agitation from voice biometrics places it squarely inside. If, and only if, one of those scope conditions or the medical/safety exception applies, the system is not thereby unregulated: emotion recognition systems are listed high‑risk under Annex III(1)(c) and are therefore high‑risk by virtue of Article 6(2), with the full Chapter III provider regime attaching, and deployers must additionally inform the natural persons exposed to the system of its operation and process the personal data in accordance with Regulations (EU) 2016/679 and (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680 under Article 50(3), an obligation disapplied only for biometric categorisation and emotion recognition permitted by law to detect, prevent or investigate criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of third parties and in accordance with Union law.

No. Adding ethnicity inference is a prohibited practice under Article 5(1)(g). That provision bans the placing on the market, the putting into service for this specific purpose, or the use of biometric categorisation systems that categorise individually natural persons based on their biometric data to deduce or infer their race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation. Inferring a shopper's ethnicity from facial or other biometric data is an inference of race within the meaning of that point (Recital 30 confirms that deducing race, alongside political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation, from a person's face or fingerprint is what the prohibition targets), and the prohibition is drafted by reference to the inferred attribute, not to the motive, so a marketing-personalisation purpose neither justifies nor narrows it. The single carve-out in Article 5(1)(g) does not assist you: it covers only labelling or filtering of lawfully acquired biometric datasets, such as images, based on biometric data, and categorising of biometric data in the area of law enforcement. Retail personalisation is neither, the operator's system categorises identified individuals in real time to drive commercial treatment, rather than sorting an already-acquired dataset (Recital 30's example of sorting images by hair or eye colour), and the operator is not a law-enforcement actor. Nor does the definitional exclusion in Article 3(40) apply: a system is outside the notion of "biometric categorisation system" only where the categorisation is ancillary to another commercial service and strictly necessary for objective technical reasons, whereas here the ethnicity inference is the personalisation feature itself and is not technically indispensable to delivering the service. Note also that the prohibition bites on the deployer's use as well as on placing on the market, so neither building nor merely operating such a feature is available; and Article 5(1)(g) applies irrespective of consent, since Article 5 admits no consent-based derogation. The consequence for the operator's existing product is that the ethnicity feature must be dropped rather than mitigated by safeguards. The age-range categorisation can continue, but it is not unregulated: a biometric categorisation system according to sensitive or protected attributes or characteristics based on the inference of those attributes falls within Annex III, point 1(b) and is therefore high-risk under Article 6(2), bringing the provider duties of Article 13 (design for transparency to deployers plus instructions for use containing the provider's identity and contact details, the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance including intended purpose, accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity levels, known or foreseeable circumstances that may lead to risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, pre-determined changes to the system, and the human-oversight measures), Article 14 human oversight, conformity assessment under Article 43 via Annex VI or Annex VII, and registration in the EU database under Article 49(1) before placing on the market or putting into service. As deployer the operator must additionally inform the natural persons exposed to the biometric categorisation system of its operation and process the personal data in accordance with Regulations (EU) 2016/679 and (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680 as applicable, that information duty being disapplied only for biometric categorisation and emotion recognition permitted by law to detect, prevent or investigate criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards and in accordance with Union law (Article 50(3)).

Yes. Reliance on the missing‑persons limb in Article 5(1), first subparagraph, point (h)(i) does not dispense with prior authorisation: Article 5(3) provides that, for the purposes of point (h) and paragraph 2, each use of a real‑time remote biometric identification system in publicly accessible spaces for law‑enforcement purposes is subject to prior authorisation granted, upon a reasoned request and in accordance with the detailed national rules referred to in Article 5(5), by a judicial authority or by an independent administrative authority whose decision is binding in the Member State where the use is to take place. The only relaxation is temporal, not substantive: in a duly justified situation of urgency the use may commence without authorisation provided authorisation is requested without undue delay and at the latest within 24 hours, and if it is refused the use must stop with immediate effect and all data, results and outputs of that use must be immediately discarded and deleted. The authorising authority may grant authorisation only if satisfied, on the basis of objective evidence or clear indications presented to it, that the use is necessary for and proportionate to achieving the point (h) objective identified in the request, here the targeted search for a missing person, and in particular remains limited to what is strictly necessary as regards the period of time and the geographic and personal scope; in deciding it must take into account the elements in Article 5(2), namely the nature of the situation giving rise to the possible use (Article 5(2)(a)) and the consequences of the use for the rights and freedoms of all persons concerned, in particular the seriousness, probability and scale of those consequences (Article 5(2)(b)). No decision producing an adverse legal effect on a person may be taken based solely on the system's output (Article 5(3)). Authorisation is also cumulative with, not a substitute for, the other conditions in Article 5(2): the use must comply with the necessary and proportionate safeguards and conditions of the authorising national law, in particular temporal, geographic and personal limitations, the law enforcement authority must have completed a fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27, and the system must have been registered in the EU database under Article 49 (with the exception, in duly justified urgency, of registration being completed without undue delay). Each use must further be notified to the relevant market surveillance authority and the national data protection authority under Article 5(4), and Article 5(1), first subparagraph, point (h) is without prejudice to Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 for processing of biometric data for non‑law‑enforcement purposes. Because these obligations sit in Chapter II, they have applied since 2 February 2025 under Article 113(3)(a), and Member States may under Article 5(5) impose stricter national rules or decline to authorise point (h) uses at all.

Annex III(4)(b) captures the system squarely, and on two independent limbs. Point 4(b) of Annex III covers AI systems intended to be used to make decisions affecting terms of work-related relationships, the promotion or termination of work-related contractual relationships, to allocate tasks based on individual behaviour or personal traits or characteristics, or to monitor and evaluate the performance and behaviour of persons in such relationships. A system that selects or ranks employees for redundancy in a restructuring is intended to be used to make decisions on the termination of work-related contractual relationships (first limb), and where it does so by scoring performance it simultaneously falls within the monitoring-and-evaluation limb. Recruitment-side tools are point 4(a); an incumbent-workforce layoff tool is 4(b), and it is irrelevant that the employer frames the exercise as collective restructuring rather than individual dismissal, the point is drafted by reference to the intended use, not the legal form of the termination. The legal consequence follows from Article 6(2): AI systems referred to in Annex III shall be considered to be high-risk. Classification does not depend on the employer's characterisation but on the system's intended purpose, so the full Chapter III regime attaches to the provider, and the Article 26 deployer duties to the employer using it. The Article 6(3) derogation is unavailable here. It applies only where the system does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making, and only where one of four conditions is fulfilled: (a) the system performs a narrow procedural task; (b) it improves the result of a previously completed human activity; (c) it detects decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns and is not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment, without proper human review; or (d) it performs a preparatory task to an assessment relevant for an Annex III use case. A system used to decide layoffs materially influences the outcome of the decision, so the chapeau already fails; and in any event, notwithstanding those conditions, an Annex III system shall always be considered high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons, which evaluating individual employees on performance, behaviour or personal characteristics will typically constitute. A provider who nonetheless considers the derogation applies must document that assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service, under Article 6(4). Two boundaries: if the tool infers emotions of employees, its use in the workplace is prohibited outright under Article 5(1)(f) save for medical or safety reasons, and prohibition displaces classification; and Article 5(1)(c) social scoring and Article 5(1)(d) criminal-offence risk assessment are not engaged by ordinary performance-based redundancy selection. Article 5(8) preserves prohibitions arising under other Union law, including employment and non-discrimination law.

No, you cannot put the system into service with a real client for genuine hiring decisions while it is in the Spanish sandbox. Participation in an AI regulatory sandbox under Article 57 provides a controlled environment for development, training, testing and validation prior to placing on the market or putting into service, under the supervision of the national competent authority and pursuant to an agreed sandbox plan; it is not a marketing authorisation, it does not suspend any requirement of Chapter III, Section 2, and it does not shield you from supervisory or corrective powers. A recruitment or candidate-evaluation system is high-risk under Article 6(2) read with Annex III, point 4, and because it profiles natural persons the Article 6(3) derogation (and with it the documented self-assessment and Article 6(4)/Article 49(2) route) is unavailable to you. Consequently, before any client may use it operationally the operator must complete, as provider, the full compliance chain: the continuous iterative risk-management system of Article 9(1)-(2), comprising identification and analysis of known and reasonably foreseeable risks, estimation and evaluation of risks arising in intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse, evaluation of risks from post-market monitoring data, and adoption of targeted risk-management measures; the data-governance practices of Article 10(2)(a)-(h), including bias examination and mitigation; the Annex IV technical documentation drawn up before placing on the market (Article 11(1)); transparency and instructions for use containing at least the Article 13(3)(a)-(f) items, including intended purpose, declared accuracy metrics, robustness and cybersecurity, foreseeable risk circumstances, explanatory capability, performance on specific persons or groups, input-data specifications, pre-determined changes, human-oversight measures, computational resources and log-collection mechanisms; human oversight under Article 14(1)-(4), including automation-bias awareness and the ability to disregard, override or intervene; Article 15 accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity; the Article 16 provider duties with the Article 17 quality-management system; the Article 43 conformity assessment; and registration in the EU database under Article 49 before placing on the market or putting into service. The only lawful way to involve real candidates beforehand is testing in real-world conditions under Article 60, expressly contemplated by Article 9(7) as part of the testing procedures, but that remains testing under its own safeguards, with the client acting as a testing partner rather than a deployer using outputs for actual recruitment outcomes.

Yes, Article 99(3) is the provision that applies to the operator's infringement, but the €35 000 000 figure is not the operator's ceiling: as an SME/start-up the operator is capped at the lower of the two limbs, i.e. 7 % of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year. Article 99(3) sets the penalty band for non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices referred to in Article 5, at up to EUR 35 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7 % of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher. That "whichever is higher" rule is expressly reversed for the operator's category by Article 99(6): in the case of SMEs, including start-ups, each fine referred to in Article 99 is up to the percentage or the amount in paragraphs 3, 4 and 5, whichever is lower. For a 25-employee company, 7 % of worldwide turnover will be far below EUR 35 million, so that percentage is the operative maximum. Two qualifications: the operator must actually meet the SME/start-up criteria as an undertaking (turnover of any linked or partner entities counts toward the "undertaking" and toward the 7 % base), and Article 99(6) caps the maximum only, it does not reduce the fine the national authority chooses within that maximum. Two further constraints cut in the operator's favour. Article 99(1) requires penalties to be effective, proportionate and dissuasive and to take into account the interests of SMEs, including start-ups, and their economic viability. Article 99(7) requires the authority, when deciding whether to impose a fine and its amount, to give due regard in each individual case to: (a) the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement and its consequences, taking into account the purpose of the AI system and, where appropriate, the number of affected persons and the level of damage; (b) whether fines have already been applied by other market surveillance authorities for the same infringement; (c) whether fines have already been applied by other authorities for infringements of other Union or national law; (d) the size, annual turnover and market share of the operator; (e) any other aggravating or mitigating factor, including financial benefits gained or losses avoided; (f) the degree of cooperation with the national competent authorities; (g) the degree of responsibility of the operator, taking into account technical and organisational measures implemented; (h) the manner in which the infringement became known, in particular whether the operator notified it; (i) the intentional or negligent character of the infringement; and (j) any action taken to mitigate the harm to affected persons. Here, limbs (a) and (i) are squarely aggravating, a knowing, six-month deployment, while (f), (h) and (j) are the levers still available to you through self-reporting, cooperation and remediation. Enforcement remains subject to the procedural safeguards in Article 99(10), including effective judicial remedies and due process, and under Article 5(8) the Article 5 prohibition does not affect prohibitions arising where the practice infringes other Union law, so parallel exposure (e.g. data-protection or employment law) is unaffected by the Article 99 ceiling. Note also that the Article 5 prohibitions have applied since 2 February 2025 under Article 113, so a six-month deployment falls within the enforceable period.

The Annex III route under Article 6(2) applies: a system falling within Annex III, point 4 is high-risk by virtue of being a listed use case, not by virtue of any product classification. The Annex I route in Article 6(1) is a different and cumulative test, it applies only where the AI system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation; employment and worker-management systems are not classified through that route unless they independently satisfy both of those conditions. Within point 4 ("Employment, workers' management and access to self-employment"), confirm which lettered use case the operator is in, because only a lettered entry triggers Article 6(2): point 4(a) covers AI systems intended to be used for the recruitment or selection of natural persons, in particular to place targeted job advertisements, to analyse and filter job applications, and to evaluate candidates; point 4(b) covers AI systems intended to be used to make decisions affecting terms of work-related relationships, the promotion or termination of work-related contractual relationships, to allocate tasks based on individual behaviour or personal traits or characteristics, or to monitor and evaluate the performance and behaviour of persons in such relationships. The only exit from that classification is the Article 6(3) derogation: the system is not high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making, and where any one of four conditions is met, (a) it performs a narrow procedural task; (b) it improves the result of a previously completed human activity; (c) it detects decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns and is not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment without proper human review; or (d) it performs a preparatory task to an assessment relevant to an Annex III use case. Notwithstanding those conditions, the system is always high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons, which will defeat the derogation for most candidate-scoring, task-allocation and performance-monitoring tools. If you do rely on the derogation, Article 6(4) requires the provider to document that assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service, subjects the provider to the registration obligation in Article 49(2), and requires the documentation to be produced to national competent authorities on request.

Annex I obligations attach to an AI system embedded in a medical device only where both cumulative conditions of Article 6(1) are met. First, under Article 6(1)(a), the AI system must be intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or itself be a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in for this sector, Annex I, point 11 (Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices) and Annex I, point 12 (Regulation (EU) 2017/746 on in vitro diagnostic medical devices). Second, under Article 6(1)(b), that product, the device whose safety component the AI system is, or the AI system itself as a product, must be required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service pursuant to that same sectoral legislation. Where the device may be self-assessed by the manufacturer without notified-body involvement under the MDR or IVDR, condition (b) fails and the Annex I route does not classify the system as high-risk. Article 6(1) applies irrespective of whether the AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of the device in which it is embedded, so an AI component supplied separately from the finished device is caught on the same terms. This route is distinct from the Annex III route: Article 6(2) makes the systems listed in Annex III high-risk on the basis of their listed use-case, and the Article 6(3) derogation, no significant risk of harm together with one of the four conditions in points (a) to (d) (narrow procedural task; improving the result of a previously completed human activity; detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the previously completed human assessment without proper human review; or a preparatory task), subject to the rule that profiling of natural persons always makes the system high-risk, and to the documentation duty in Article 6(4), operates only "by derogation from paragraph 2". It is therefore unavailable to a system classified as high-risk through Annex I, which remains high-risk whenever the two conditions of Article 6(1) are satisfied. A medical AI system may of course also fall under a listed Annex III use-case independently, for instance emergency healthcare patient triage under Annex III, point 5(d).

No. Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as adopted, the version applicable here, the transitional dates in Article 111 are unchanged: AI systems that are components of the large-scale IT systems established by the acts listed in Annex X and placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2027 must be brought into compliance by 31 December 2030 (Article 111(1)); high-risk AI systems placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2026 are caught only where their design changes significantly thereafter, with public-authority deployers required to comply by 2 August 2030 (Article 111(2)); and providers of general-purpose AI models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 must take the necessary steps to comply by 2 August 2027 (Article 111(3)). Nothing in the adopted text postpones those dates, and the Article 5 prohibitions continue to apply from their own date without a transitional grace period, as Article 111(1) expressly preserves. The Digital Omnibus is a later legislative initiative outside the corpus of the Regulation as adopted; any deferral it might introduce would take effect only through an adopted amending act and cannot be read into this version. If you need the position under current law rather than the as-adopted text, that must be assessed against the amending instrument itself, which is not part of the material I am applying here.

Not signing the Code of Practice is permissible: adherence under Article 56 is one route to demonstrating compliance, not the source of the duties themselves, and Article 53(4) expressly provides two alternatives. First, you may comply with a European harmonised standard, compliance with such standards grants a presumption of conformity to the extent those standards cover the Article 53(1) obligations (at present no such standard has been published for GPAI, so this route is not yet available in practice). Second, and failing either adherence to an approved code of practice or compliance with a harmonised standard, Article 53(4) requires the operator to "demonstrate alternative adequate means of compliance for assessment by the Commission", i.e. the operator must be able to evidence, in a form the Commission (through the AI Office) can assess, that each Article 53(1) obligation is met: the Annex XI technical documentation kept up to date including the training and testing process and evaluation results (Article 53(1)(a)); the Annex XII information made available to downstream providers so they can understand the model's capabilities and limitations and meet their own obligations (Article 53(1)(b)(i), (ii)); a policy to comply with Union copyright law (Article 53(1)(c)); and a publicly available sufficiently detailed summary of the training content (Article 53(1)(d)). Note that Article 53(1)(a) and (b) do not apply to models released under a free and open-source licence allowing access, use, modification and distribution with publicly available parameters, weights, architecture and usage information, but that exception does not extend to models with systemic risk (Article 53(2)); the copyright policy and training-data summary apply regardless. If the operator's model is classified as a GPAI model with systemic risk under Article 51(1)(a), (b), presumed where cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs (Article 51(2)), the same structure applies one layer up: Article 55(2) mirrors Article 53(4), so non-adherence obliges the operator to demonstrate alternative adequate means of compliance, for Commission assessment, with each Article 55(1) obligation: model evaluation under standardised protocols and tools reflecting the state of the art, including documented adversarial testing (Article 55(1)(a)); assessment and mitigation of possible Union-level systemic risks and their sources arising from development, placing on the market or use (Article 55(1)(b)); tracking, documenting and reporting without undue delay to the AI Office, and where appropriate national competent authorities, serious incidents and possible corrective measures (Article 55(1)(c)); and an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure (Article 55(1)(d)). Information and documentation you submit, including trade secrets, is protected by the confidentiality regime of Article 78 (Articles 53(7), 55(3)). Two further points bear on the choice. Article 56(7) allows the AI Office to invite providers to adhere, and for providers without systemic risk that adherence may be limited to the Article 53 obligations unless they explicitly declare an interest in joining the full code, so partial, Article 53-only adherence is a middle path rather than an all-or-nothing decision. And under Article 56(9), if the Commission deems a code inadequate or it cannot be finalised, the Commission may lay down common rules for implementing Articles 53 and 55 by implementing act under the Article 98(2) examination procedure; such rules would be binding irrespective of the operator's signature status. The practical consequence of the non-signatory route is evidentiary, not substantive: you carry the burden of constructing and maintaining a compliance dossier that the Commission can assess on its own terms, without the benefit of the code's structured presumption.

No. Article 88 is not a fining provision, and the AI Office is not itself the fining authority: Article 88(1) confers on the Commission exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V, subject to the procedural guarantees of Article 94, and provides that the Commission shall entrust the implementation of those tasks to the AI Office, without prejudice to the Commission's powers of organisation and the Treaty-based division of competences between the Union and the Member States. The AI Office therefore acts as the Commission's internal structure for GPAI supervision (Article 64(1)), but the legal act imposing a fine is a Commission decision, and its legal basis is Article 101, not Article 88. Under Article 101(1), the Commission may impose on providers of general-purpose AI models fines not exceeding 3 % of their annual total worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher, where it finds that the provider intentionally or negligently: (a) infringed the relevant provisions of the Regulation; (b) failed to comply with a request for a document or for information pursuant to Article 91, or supplied incorrect, incomplete or misleading information; (c) failed to comply with a measure requested under Article 93; or (d) failed to make available access to the general-purpose AI model, or general-purpose AI model with systemic risk, with a view to an evaluation pursuant to Article 92. In fixing the amount, regard must be had to the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement, with due account of proportionality and appropriateness, and account must also be taken of commitments made under Article 93(3) or in codes of practice under Article 56. The accompanying safeguards are part of the same rule: before adopting a decision under paragraph 1 the Commission must communicate its preliminary findings to the provider and give it an opportunity to be heard (Article 101(2)); fines must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive (Article 101(3)); information on fines is communicated to the Board as appropriate (Article 101(4)); the Court of Justice has unlimited jurisdiction to review, and may cancel, reduce or increase, a fine fixed under this Article (Article 101(5)); and the detailed arrangements and procedural safeguards are laid down in implementing acts adopted under the examination procedure of Article 98(2) (Article 101(6)). Correspondingly, national market surveillance authorities have no fining power over GPAI model providers in respect of Chapter V; without prejudice to Article 75(3), they may only request the Commission to exercise the powers laid down in that Section where necessary and proportionate to assist with their own tasks (Article 88(2)).

No retrofitting is required: a high-risk AI system placed on the market in March 2026 is grandfathered under Article 111(2), because that Regulation applies to operators of high-risk systems placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2026 only if, as from that date, those systems become subject to significant changes in their designs. That relief is, however, qualified in four respects, and all of them must be tracked. First, the grandfathering lapses the moment the system undergoes a significant change in its design on or after 2 August 2026; from that point the full high-risk regime, risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, transparency to deployers, conformity assessment and CE marking, registration and post-market obligations, applies in the ordinary way, so the exemption is best treated as a design freeze rather than a permanent exclusion. Second, if the system is intended to be used by public authorities, Article 111(2) imposes an absolute backstop: providers and deployers must in any case take the necessary steps to comply with the requirements and obligations of the Regulation by 2 August 2030, irrespective of whether any design change occurs. Third, Article 111(2) operates without prejudice to Article 5 as referred to in Article 113(3), point (a); the prohibited-practices regime binds the system regardless of when it was placed on the market, so grandfathering offers no shelter there. Fourth, Article 111(2) covers high-risk systems "other than the systems referred to in paragraph 1", so if the operator's system is a component of one of the large-scale IT systems established by the acts listed in Annex X (the Schengen Information System, the Visa Information System, Eurodac, the Entry/Exit System, ETIAS, ECRIS-TCN, and the interoperability Regulations), the March 2026 placing falls before 2 August 2027 and the applicable compliance date is 31 December 2030 under Article 111(1) instead. Two scoping points determine which limb applies. The classification route is not affected by the transitional rule: the operator's system is high-risk either as a safety component of, or as, a product covered by the Annex I harmonisation legislation that must undergo third-party conformity assessment (Article 6(1)), or because it falls within a lettered use-case under one of the eight Annex III areas (Article 6(2)). Either way, Article 111(2) attaches to the date of placing on the market, not to the route. And if you instead conclude that the system is not high-risk under the Article 6(3) derogation, that is a different analysis requiring documented self-assessment before placing on the market plus registration under Article 49(2), it is not what Article 111 provides.

No. Article 13 imposes no obligation to give the rejected loan applicant reasons for the denial; it is a provider-facing design and documentation duty owed to the deployer, not a duty owed to the affected natural person. Article 13(1) requires that the high-risk system be designed and developed so that its operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret the system's output and use it appropriately, with an appropriate type and degree of transparency to achieve compliance with the provider's and deployer's obligations under Section 3. Article 13(2) requires the system to be accompanied by instructions for use, in an appropriate digital format or otherwise, containing concise, complete, correct and clear information that is relevant, accessible and comprehensible to deployers. Article 13(3) fixes the contents of those instructions in full: (a) the identity and contact details of the provider; (b) the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance, comprising (i) the intended purpose, (ii) the level of accuracy including its metrics, robustness and cybersecurity referred to in Article 15 against which the system was tested and validated and any known and foreseeable circumstances affecting that expected level, (iii) any known or foreseeable circumstance, in use according to the intended purpose or under reasonably foreseeable misuse, which may lead to risks to health and safety or fundamental rights referred to in Article 9(2), (iv) where applicable, the technical capabilities and characteristics of the system to provide information relevant to explain its output, (v) when appropriate, performance regarding specific persons or groups on which the system is intended to be used, (vi) when appropriate, input-data specifications or other relevant information on the training, validation and testing data sets, and (vii) where applicable, information enabling deployers to interpret the output and use it appropriately; (c) changes to the system and its performance pre-determined by the provider at the time of the initial conformity assessment; (d) the human oversight measures, including technical measures to facilitate interpretation of outputs by deployers; (e) the computational and hardware resources needed, the expected lifetime and the necessary maintenance and care measures; and (f) where relevant, a description of the mechanisms allowing deployers to properly collect, store and interpret the logs in accordance with Article 12. The point closest to the operator's question, Article 13(3)(b)(iv), is only a disclosure to the deployer about whether and how the system can produce output-explaining information, it is an input to the operator's explanation capability, not an obligation to deliver reasons to the applicant. Likewise Article 13(3)(b)(vii) equips you to interpret the score internally. The individual-facing duty that does bind you as deployer of a creditworthiness-evaluation system, high-risk under Article 6(2) read with Annex III, point 5(b), is Article 26(11): as a deployer of an Annex III high-risk system that makes decisions or assists in making decisions relating to natural persons, the operator must inform the natural persons that they are subject to the use of the high-risk AI system, without prejudice to Article 50. That is a notification duty about exposure to the system, not a duty to state the reasons for the denial. Article 50(6) further provides that Article 50(1), (4) do not affect the Chapter III requirements and are without prejudice to other transparency obligations laid down in Union or national law for deployers, so any obligation to state reasons for the individual credit decision must be sourced outside including in the other Union and national rules that Article 50(6) expressly preserves. The operator's remaining Article 26 duties around the decision remain: use in accordance with the instructions for use (Article 26(1)), human oversight by competent, trained natural persons (Article 26(2)), monitoring on the basis of the instructions for use with incident reporting under Article 26(5), and log retention for at least six months under Article 26(6), with the qualification that if the operator is a financial institution subject to internal-governance requirements under Union financial services law, the Article 26(5) monitoring obligation and the Article 26(6) log-retention obligation are fulfilled by complying with those internal-governance rules.

A separate person or entity established in the Union, appointed by the US parent under a written mandate, plays that role, the third-country provider cannot perform the function itself, and nothing in the Regulation lets the absence of an EU establishment excuse the appointment. Prior to making a high-risk AI system available on the Union market, a provider established in a third country must, by written mandate, appoint an authorised representative established in the Union (Article 22(1)); where the group has no EU subsidiary or branch, that mandate must be given to an independent natural or legal person established in a Member State (for example an EU-based compliance service provider or an EU distributor or importer willing to accept the mandate), since establishment in the Union is the only qualifying criterion. The provider must enable the representative to perform the mandated tasks (Article 22(2)). The mandate must cover the tasks in Article 22(3): verifying that the EU declaration of conformity and the technical documentation have been drawn up and that an appropriate conformity assessment procedure has been carried out by the provider (point (a)); keeping at the disposal of the competent authorities and national authorities, for 10 years after the system has been placed on the market or put into service, the contact details of the appointing provider, a copy of the mandate, the EU declaration of conformity, the technical documentation and, where applicable, the certificate issued by the notified body (point (b)); providing a competent authority, on reasoned request, with all information and documentation necessary to demonstrate conformity, including access to the logs automatically generated by the system and under the provider's control (point (c)); cooperating with competent authorities on any action they take in relation to the high-risk AI system, in particular to reduce and mitigate the risks it poses (point (d)); and, where applicable, complying with the registration obligations under Article 49(1) or, where the provider registers itself, ensuring that the information in point 3 of Section A of Annex VIII is correct (point (e)). The mandate must empower the representative to be addressed, in addition to or instead of the provider, by the competent authorities on all issues relating to compliance with the Regulation. The representative is not a substitute provider: the substantive duties, risk management (Article 9), data governance (Article 10), technical documentation (Article 11), logging (Article 12), transparency and instructions for use (Article 13), human oversight (Article 14), accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity (Article 15), the quality management system (Article 17), conformity assessment (Article 43), the declaration of conformity (Article 47), CE marking (Article 48), post-market monitoring (Article 72) and serious-incident reporting (Article 73), remain with the US parent as provider. The representative's identity and contact details must appear in the instructions for use alongside the provider's (Article 13(3)(a)) and in the EU declaration of conformity (Annex V). Registration in the EU database before placing on the market or putting into service may be carried out by the provider or, where applicable, the authorised representative, both for Annex III high-risk systems other than those in point 2 of Annex III (Article 49(1)) and for systems the provider has concluded are not high-risk under Article 6(3) (Article 49(2)). Finally, the representative must terminate the mandate if it considers, or has reason to consider, that the provider is acting contrary to its obligations under the Regulation, and must then immediately inform the relevant market surveillance authority and, where applicable, the relevant notified body of the termination and its reasons (Article 22(4)).

branch_rows.pred_answer: Adding facial-expression engagement scoring for the operator's own employees is not a "risk level" question at all, it is a prohibited AI practice. Article 5(1)(f) forbids the placing on the market, putting into service for this specific purpose, or use of AI systems to infer emotions of a natural person in the areas of workplace and education institutions, and the only carve-out is where the system is intended to be put in place or into the market for medical or safety reasons. Scoring staff "engagement" during internal meetings is a workplace productivity/management purpose, not a medical or safety one, so the derogation is unavailable and the feature cannot lawfully be built or run. It is equally irrelevant that the tool is internal and never sold: putting a system into service for the operator's own use, under the operator's own name, makes you its provider (Article 25), and Article 5 binds providers and deployers alike, including purely in-house use on the operator's own staff. Because the practice is prohibited, no downstream compliance route cures it. You cannot reach it by treating the feature as an Annex III high-risk employment or biometrics use and discharging Articles 9 to 15, 43 and 47 to 49; nor does the deployer transparency duty in Article 50(3), informing exposed persons of the operation of an emotion recognition system and processing their personal data accordingly, render an otherwise banned workplace use lawful, since Article 50 is without prejudice to the Chapter II prohibition. Employee consent does not cure it either, as Article 5 admits no consent-based exception. Drop the facial-expression feature. The meeting-summarisation function itself remains outside Article 5, subject to the operator's Article 4 AI literacy duty for staff operating it.

The system must pass the conformity assessment procedure based on internal control under Annex VI, carried out by the provider itself with no notified body involved. A CV-sorting system for recruitment is an Annex III point 4(a) employment use-case and is therefore high-risk under Article 6(2); because it falls outside Annex III point 1 (biometrics), Article 43(2) applies directly and mandates the Annex VI route for all Annex III points 2 to 8, the Annex VII notified-body option and the harmonised-standards/common-specifications choice in Article 43(1) are confined to point 1 systems and are not open to you, and the Article 43(3) sectoral route applies only to Annex I products. Under Annex VI that internal-control procedure has three operative steps, all of which must be completed before placing on the market: verifying that the established quality management system complies with Article 17 (Annex VI.2); examining the information in the technical documentation to assess the system's compliance with the essential requirements of Chapter III, Section 2 (Annex VI.3); and verifying that the design and development process and the post-market monitoring under Article 72 are consistent with that technical documentation (Annex VI.4). The technical documentation itself must be drawn up before placing on the market, kept up to date, and contain at least the Annex IV elements, in a form allowing national competent authorities and notified bodies to assess compliance (Article 11(1)). Conformity is then demonstrated by the provider's own acts under Article 16(1): ensuring the system undergoes the Article 43 procedure prior to placing on the market or putting into service (point (f)), drawing up the EU declaration of conformity in accordance with Article 47 (point (g)), affixing the CE marking to the system or, where that is not possible, to its packaging or accompanying documentation in accordance with Article 48 (point (h)), complying with the registration obligations in Article 49(1) (point (i)), keeping the Article 18 documentation (point (d)), and, upon a reasoned request of a national competent authority, demonstrating the conformity of the system with the Section 2 requirements (point (k)). That evidentiary duty is specified in Article 21: on reasoned request the operator must supply all information and documentation necessary to demonstrate conformity with Section 2, in an official Union language easily understood by the authority as indicated by the Member State concerned (Article 21(1)), and give access to the automatically generated logs referred to in Article 12(1) to the extent they are under the operator's control (Article 21(2)), with the information received treated under the Article 78 confidentiality obligations (Article 21(3)). Two follow-on points bind after first assessment. A substantial modification triggers a new conformity assessment, regardless of whether the modified system is further distributed or continues to be used by the current deployer; changes to the system and its performance that you pre-determined at the moment of the initial conformity assessment and included in the Annex IV point 2(f) technical documentation do not constitute a substantial modification (Article 43(4)), and those pre-determined changes must also be stated in the instructions for use (Article 13(3)(c)). Separately, if you took the view that the system is not high-risk under an Article 6(3) derogation, that assessment would have to be documented before placing on the market with registration under Article 49(2) (Article 6(4)), but a recruitment CV-sorting tool that ranks or filters candidates is not a narrow procedural, human-result-improving, pattern-detection or preparatory task, so that route is not available here.

Yes, 3×10²⁵ FLOPs changes the operator's classification. Because the cumulative amount of computation used for training, measured in floating-point operations, is greater than 10²⁵, the operator's model is presumed to have high-impact capabilities under Article 51(2) and is therefore classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk under Article 51(1)(a). The presumption attaches automatically on crossing the threshold; the second, independent route in Article 51(1)(b), a Commission decision, taken ex officio or after a qualified alert from the scientific panel, that the model has capabilities or impact equivalent to point (a) having regard to the Annex XIII criteria, is not needed here, and Article 51(3) allows the Commission to amend those thresholds and supplement benchmarks and indicators by delegated act in light of algorithmic improvements or increased hardware efficiency. The consequence is cumulative, not substitutive. You remain subject to the full set of Article 53(1) provider obligations: drawing up and keeping up to date the technical documentation of the model, including its training and testing process and the results of its evaluation, per Annex XI (53(1)(a)); drawing up, keeping up to date and making available information and documentation to providers of AI systems intending to integrate the model, so as to enable them to understand its capabilities and limitations and comply with their own obligations, containing at a minimum the Annex XII elements (53(1)(b)(i), (ii)); putting in place a policy to comply with Union copyright law (53(1)(c)); and making publicly available a sufficiently detailed summary of the content used for training (53(1)(d)). On top of those, Article 55(1) adds four further duties specific to systemic risk: (a) performing model evaluation in accordance with standardised protocols and tools reflecting the state of the art, including conducting and documenting adversarial testing with a view to identifying and mitigating systemic risks; (b) assessing and mitigating possible systemic risks at Union level, including their sources, stemming from the development, placing on the market or use of the model; (c) keeping track of, documenting and reporting, without undue delay, to the AI Office and, as appropriate, to national competent authorities, relevant information about serious incidents and possible corrective measures; and (d) ensuring an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for both the model and its physical infrastructure. Information obtained under Article 55 is covered by the Article 78 confidentiality regime (Article 55(3)). One carve-out is lost by this classification: the free and open-source exemption in Article 53(2), which would otherwise disapply the Article 53(1)(a) technical-documentation and 53(1)(b) downstream-information duties for models released under a licence permitting access, usage, modification and distribution with publicly available parameters, weights, architecture and usage information, expressly does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk. The copyright policy and the public training-data summary apply in any event. Until a harmonised standard is published you may rely on an Article 56 code of practice to demonstrate compliance with Article 53(1); compliance with a European harmonised standard grants a presumption of conformity to the extent it covers those obligations, and if you neither adhere to an approved code nor comply with such a standard the operator must demonstrate alternative adequate means of compliance for assessment by the Commission (Article 53(4)). Two qualifications on scope. First, Article 51(2) creates a presumption, not an irrebuttable rule, it is open to you to argue, on appropriate technical tools and methodologies including indicators and benchmarks, that the model does not in fact have high-impact capabilities within the meaning of Article 3(64), but until that is accepted the systemic-risk obligations apply. Second, the 3×10²⁵ figure bears on the model layer only; whether any AI system you build on the model is high-risk turns separately on Article 6 and, on that route, on the Annex III listed use-cases or the Annex I product route, which the compute figure does not affect.

Yes, the operator's legal role changes: by substantially modifying the system and placing the operator's own name or trademark on it, the operator is considered a provider of that high-risk AI system and assume the full provider obligations, while remaining a deployer in respect of the operator's own use. Two independent limbs of Article 25(1) are each satisfied here. Under Article 25(1)(b), any distributor, importer, deployer or other third party becomes a provider where it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service, without prejudice to contractual arrangements allocating obligations otherwise. Under Article 25(1)(c), the same consequence follows where such an actor makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service in such a way that it remains high-risk, a substantial modification being a change not foreseen or planned in the original provider's initial conformity assessment which affects compliance with the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements or results in a modification of the intended purpose. Re-training or re-architecting the credit-scoring model beyond the pre-determined changes documented under Article 13(3)(c) falls within that. The consequence under Article 25(2) is that the original third-party provider ceases to be the provider of that specific system, and must closely cooperate with you, make available the necessary information and the reasonably expected technical access and other assistance required for you to fulfil the obligations of the Regulation, in particular for conformity assessment, unless it has clearly excluded the change from a high-risk transformation in its instructions for use. Practically, the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements now bind you as provider, not merely as recipient: the documented, iterative risk-management system across the lifecycle (Article 9(1), (10)); data governance for training, validation and testing data sets, which must be relevant, sufficiently representative, to the best extent possible free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose, with bias examination and mitigation (Article 10(1), (5)); technical documentation drawn up before placing on the market and kept up to date, with the Annex IV content (Article 11(1)); design for operational transparency and instructions for use containing provider identity and contact details, the system's characteristics, capabilities and limitations (intended purpose; accuracy levels and metrics, robustness and cybersecurity; known or foreseeable risk circumstances; explainability capabilities; performance regarding specific persons or groups; input-data specifications; output-interpretation information), pre-determined changes, human oversight measures, computational and hardware resources, expected lifetime and maintenance, and log mechanisms (Article 13(1), (3)); effective human oversight by design (Article 14(1), (5)); and appropriate accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, with accuracy metrics declared in the instructions for use and resilience against errors, faults, feedback loops, data and model poisoning, adversarial examples, and confidentiality attacks (Article 15(1), (5)). A fresh conformity assessment, EU declaration of conformity, CE marking and Annex III registration follow. Classification is unaffected: credit scoring remains high-risk under Article 6(2) and Annex III, point 5(b) (evaluating creditworthiness or establishing credit scores of natural persons, other than for detecting financial fraud), and the Article 6(3) derogation is unavailable because a system performing profiling of natural persons is always high-risk. The operator's deployer duties do not disappear for the operator's own operational use: Article 26(1), (12) continues to require use in accordance with the instructions, assignment of human oversight to competent, trained and supported natural persons, input-data relevance, monitoring and suspension plus reporting on serious-incident or risk indications, log retention, informing affected natural persons that they are subject to the system (Article 26(11)), and use of the Article 13 information for any DPIA (Article 26(9)). Because the system is an Annex III, point 5(b) credit-scoring system, the operator must also complete a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use under Article 27(1), covering the deployment processes and intended purpose, the period and frequency of use, the categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected, the specific risks of harm to them, the human oversight measures, and the measures to be taken if those risks materialise, notifying the market surveillance authority of the result.

Yes, the classification changes. In its current form the chatbot is not high-risk; telling users they are interacting with an AI system discharges the Article 50 transparency duty and nothing more. Adding automated scoring of final exams and pass/fail determination brings the system squarely within Annex III, point 3 (education and vocational training), specifically point 3(b), AI systems intended to evaluate learning outcomes, including where those outcomes steer the learning process, and, where the pass decision governs progression, point 3(c), assessing the level of education an individual will receive or be able to access. A listed Annex III use-case makes the system high-risk under Article 6(2), and the Article 50 disclosure you already make does not displace that. The Article 6(3) derogation will not rescue it. That derogation requires no significant risk of harm plus one of four conditions: a narrow procedural task, improving the result of a previously completed human activity, detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing human assessment, or a preparatory task to an assessment. A system that itself produces the mark and the pass decision replaces the human assessment rather than preparing or refining it, and if it profiles natural persons it is high-risk in every case. If you nonetheless conclude the derogation applies, Article 6(4) obliges the operator to document that assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service, to register under Article 49(2), and to produce the documentation on request. Because the operator is modifying the intended purpose of a system already on the market so that it becomes high-risk, Article 25(1)(c) confirms you carry the full provider obligations of Article 16: conformity with the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements (including Article 10 data governance and Article 15 accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, with accuracy metrics declared in the instructions for use), provider identification, a quality-management system, technical documentation, retention of automatically generated logs, conformity assessment under Article 43, the EU declaration of conformity, CE marking, registration in the EU database, corrective action, and demonstration of conformity on request. The operator's customers become deployers under Article 26, and education institutions that are public bodies or private entities providing public services must also carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use under Article 27(1).

Before placing a high-risk AI system on the Union market, the operator must ensure it conforms with the Regulation by verifying four things: that the relevant conformity assessment procedure referred to in Article 43 has been carried out by the provider; that the provider has drawn up the technical documentation in accordance with Article 11 and Annex IV; that the system bears the required CE marking and is accompanied by the EU declaration of conformity referred to in Article 47 and the instructions for use; and that the provider has appointed an authorised representative in accordance with Article 22(1) (Article 23(1)(a), (d)). That last check bites only where the provider is established in a third country, since it is such providers who must, prior to making the system available on the Union market, appoint an established-in-the-Union authorised representative by written mandate, the mandate empowering it inter alia to verify that the declaration of conformity and technical documentation were drawn up and an appropriate conformity assessment carried out (Article 22(1) and (3)(a)). The verification duty carries a follow-on step: where you have sufficient reason to consider that the system is not in conformity, or is falsified, or is accompanied by falsified documentation, the operator must not place it on the market until it has been brought into conformity, and where the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1) the operator must inform the provider, the authorised representative and the market surveillance authorities (Article 23(2)). Two further pre-placing duties attach to you directly: the operator must indicate the operator's name, registered trade name or registered trade mark, and the address at which the operator can be contacted on the system and on its packaging or accompanying documentation, where applicable (Article 23(3)); and the operator must ensure that, while the system is under the operator's responsibility, storage or transport conditions, where applicable, do not jeopardise its compliance with the Section 2 requirements (Article 23(4)).

No. Article 26 imposes no free‑standing pre‑deployment assessment on you; the pre‑deployment assessment the operator's authority must carry out is the fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27(1), and Article 26 adds only operational duties plus two pre‑use checks. The operator's system is high‑risk on the Annex III route (Article 6(2)) as an Annex III, point 5(a) system used by a public authority to evaluate eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, including to grant, reduce, revoke or reclaim them. Because the operator is a body governed by public law deploying an Article 6(2) system, Article 27(1) requires you, before putting the system into use, to perform a fundamental rights impact assessment covering: a description of the operator's processes in which the system will be used in line with its intended purpose (Article 27(1)(a)); the period of time within which, and frequency with which, it is intended to be used (Article 27(1)(b)); the categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected in the operator's specific context (Article 27(1)(c)); the specific risks of harm likely to have an impact on those categories, taking account of the provider's Article 13 information (Article 27(1)(d)); the human oversight measures, according to the instructions for use (Article 27(1)(e)); and the measures to be taken if those risks materialise, including internal governance arrangements and complaint mechanisms (Article 27(1)(f)). The only carve‑out from that duty, high‑risk systems intended for the Annex III, point 2 critical‑infrastructure area, does not apply to housing benefit eligibility. The obligation applies to the first use; for similar subsequent deployments you may rely on the existing assessment, updating it where any of the listed elements has changed or is no longer up to date (Article 27(2)). Where any of those elements is already met through a data protection impact assessment, the fundamental rights impact assessment complements that assessment (Article 27(4)). Once performed, the operator must notify the market surveillance authority of the results, submitting the filled‑out template referred to in Article 27(5), unless the operator is exempted from that notification obligation (Article 27(3)). Under Article 26 itself, two obligations bite before or at the point of use rather than being assessments: as a public authority deployer the operator must verify that the system is registered in the EU database in accordance with Article 49, and where it is not, the operator must not use it and must inform the provider or distributor (Article 26(8)); and the operator must inform the natural persons subject to a decision made or assisted by the system that they are subject to its use (Article 26(11)). Article 26(9) does not create a new assessment either, it requires you, where applicable, to use the information provided under Article 13 to comply with the operator's Article 35 GDPR data protection impact assessment obligation, which for eligibility decisions on benefits will ordinarily be triggered. The remaining Article 26 duties are continuing ones: use the system in accordance with the instructions for use through appropriate technical and organisational measures (Article 26(1)); assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training, authority and support (Article 26(2)); ensure, to the extent you control the input data, that it is relevant and sufficiently representative in view of the intended purpose (Article 26(4)); monitor operation on the basis of the instructions for use, suspend use and inform the provider and the market surveillance authority where you identify a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1) or a serious incident (Article 26(5)); keep the automatically generated logs under the operator's control for at least six months, unless Union or national law provides otherwise (Article 26(6)); and cooperate with the relevant competent authorities (Article 26(12)). Article 4 separately requires the operator to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among the caseworkers operating the system.

Article 10 requires a documented set of data-governance steps applied to the training, validation and testing data sets of a high-risk AI system that is developed with model training, and appropriate to its intended purpose (Article 10(1) and 10(2)). Concretely, the operator's data-governance and management practices must cover each of the following: the relevant design choices; the data collection processes and the origin of the data, and, where personal data are involved, the original purpose of the collection; the relevant data-preparation processing operations such as annotation, labelling, cleaning, updating, enrichment and aggregation; the formulation of assumptions, in particular about what the data are supposed to measure and represent; an assessment of the availability, quantity and suitability of the data sets that are needed; examination in view of possible biases that are likely to affect health and safety of persons, have a negative impact on fundamental rights or lead to discrimination, in particular where data outputs influence inputs for future operations; appropriate measures to detect, prevent and mitigate those identified biases; and identification of relevant data gaps or shortcomings that prevent compliance, together with how those gaps and shortcomings can be addressed (Article 10(2)(a), (h)). On quality substance, the data sets must be relevant, sufficiently representative and, to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose, and must have the appropriate statistical properties, including, where applicable, as regards the persons or groups of persons in relation to whom the system is intended to be used; those characteristics may be satisfied at the level of individual data sets or of a combination of them (Article 10(3)). The data sets must also take into account, to the extent required by the intended purpose, the characteristics or elements particular to the specific geographical, contextual, behavioural or functional setting in which the system is to be used (Article 10(4)). Where bias detection and correction genuinely require special categories of personal data (the GDPR Article 9 categories), you may process them only to the extent strictly necessary and only subject to all of the cumulative safeguards: that bias detection and correction cannot be effectively fulfilled by processing other data, including synthetic or anonymised data; that the special-category data are subject to technical limitations on re-use and state-of-the-art security and privacy-preserving measures, including pseudonymisation; that they are subject to measures ensuring they are secured, protected and subject to suitable safeguards, including strict controls and documentation of access, to avoid misuse and ensure that only authorised persons with appropriate confidentiality obligations have access; that they are not transmitted, transferred or otherwise accessed by other parties; that they are deleted once the bias has been corrected or the personal data reach the end of their retention period, whichever comes first; and that the records of processing activities include the reasons why processing special categories of personal data was strictly necessary to detect and correct biases and why that objective could not be achieved by processing other data (Article 10(5) and 10(5)(a), (f)). If the high-risk system does not involve the training of AI models, these obligations in paragraphs 2 to 5 apply only to the testing data sets (Article 10(6)). Operationally, these steps must be carried inside the operator's quality management system as documented systems and procedures for data management, data acquisition, collection, analysis, labelling, storage, filtration, mining, aggregation and retention, and any other operation performed before and for the purpose of placing the system on the market or putting it into service (Article 17(1)(f)), and residual bias and data-related risks must be fed into the iterative risk-management process, including the adoption of targeted risk-management measures (Article 9(2)(a) and (d)).

Treat this as a serious incident and act now on three parallel tracks, suspend and report, preserve the logs, and inform the affected patient, because an emergency healthcare patient triage system is a high-risk AI system under Article 6(2) read with Annex III, point 5 (the use-case covering systems used to establish priority in the dispatching of emergency first response services and emergency healthcare patient triage), and serious deterioration of a person's health is a "serious incident" within Article 3(49). As deployer, Article 26(5) requires the operator to monitor operation on the basis of the instructions for use and, where you have reason to consider that use in accordance with those instructions may present a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), to inform the provider (or distributor) and the relevant market surveillance authority without delay and to suspend use of the system. Suspension is not discretionary once that threshold is reached; if the mis-triage instead arose because the system was used outside the instructions for use, the failure is the operator's own under Article 26(1), which obliges the operator to take appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure use in accordance with those instructions, and the corrective action lies on the organisational side. Either way, the operator must inform the provider of the serious incident under Article 26(5). Secure the logs immediately. Article 26(6) requires the operator to keep the logs automatically generated by the system, to the extent they are under the operator's control, for a period appropriate to the intended purpose and in any event at least six months, unless Union or national law, in particular data protection law, provides otherwise; the provider has the mirror duty under Article 16(1)(e). The logs covering the triage episode are the evidentiary basis for the provider's incident investigation, for any market surveillance evaluation, and for the patient's explanation right, so they must be ring-fenced against routine deletion or overwriting now, not after the investigation concludes. Reporting deadlines run from awareness, so a harm that occurred last week is already inside the operative window. Where the triage system is not a device regulated under Regulation (EU) 2017/745 or (EU) 2017/746, the provider must report the serious incident to the market surveillance authority of the Member State where it occurred under Article 73: immediately once a causal link between the AI system and the serious incident, or the reasonable likelihood of such a link, is established and in any event no later than 15 days after becoming aware of the serious incident; no later than 10 days after the date of awareness in the event of the death of a person; and immediately, and not later than 2 days after awareness, in the case of a widespread infringement or a serious and irreversible disruption of the management or operation of critical infrastructure. If the operator's triage system is itself a medical device or a safety component of one, Article 73's dual-reporting exemption narrows rather than adds to the duty: patient death or serious deterioration of health routes through the manufacturer's vigilance reporting under Regulation (EU) 2017/745, and the AI Act notification is confined to an infringement of Union law protecting fundamental rights, made to the national competent authority designated for that purpose. Identify which track applies before you file, because filing generic "15 days to the market surveillance authority" is wrong for a regulated device. The patient has an enforceable right against you as deployer. Under Article 86, a person subject to a decision taken by the deployer on the basis of output from an Annex III high-risk system that produces legal effects or similarly significantly adverse effects on health, safety or fundamental rights may obtain from you a clear and meaningful explanation of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken. That right is subject to two limits: it does not apply where exceptions or restrictions follow from Union or national law in compliance with Union law (Article 86(2)), and it applies only to the extent the right is not otherwise provided for under Union law (Article 86(3)), so where national health law or data protection law already supplies an equivalent explanation, that channel governs, but silence in the patient record is not a defence. Finally, expect the regulatory consequence. Once notified, the market surveillance authority will evaluate the system under Article 79 and, on a finding of non-compliance, will require corrective action within a period proportionate to the risk, bringing the system into compliance, withdrawal from the market, recall, or restriction of its availability, and will inform the Commission and the other Member States. Prepare the incident file, the human-oversight record for the triage episode, and the instructions-for-use compliance evidence on the assumption that it will be requested.

Article 86 grants the applicant that right. A loan-decisioning system that evaluates the creditworthiness of natural persons or establishes their credit score is a high-risk AI system under the Annex III route (Article 6(2), Annex III, point 5(b), the only carve-out there being systems used to detect financial fraud), so the denial is a decision taken by you as deployer on the basis of output from an Annex III high-risk system.
