Under Article 86, any affected person subject to such a decision, where it produces legal effects or similarly significantly adversely affects that person's health, safety or fundamental rights, has the right to obtain from the deployer clear and meaningful explanation of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken. The duty is owed by you, the deployer, not by the provider. Its limits are: it does not extend to Annex III, point 2 (critical infrastructure) systems; it applies only where the person is subject to a decision producing legal effects or similarly significant adverse effects; and it operates without prejudice to, and does not displace, the rights and safeguards under Article 22 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679, nor exceptions or restrictions flowing from other Union or national law. Confidential business information and trade-secret protection under Article 78 and Article 25(5) may shape how the explanation is framed, but cannot be used to defeat the Article 86 right itself. Two adjacent duties apply to the same interaction. Under Article 26(11), as a deployer of an Annex III high-risk system making or assisting in decisions about natural persons, the operator must inform the applicant that they are subject to the use of the high-risk AI system, a proactive notice duty, distinct from the on-request explanation in Article 86. The operator's ability to give that explanation should be drawn from the provider's instructions for use under Article 13(3)(b), in particular the technical capabilities and characteristics of the system to provide information relevant to explain its output (point (b)(iv)) and the information enabling you to interpret its output and use it appropriately (point (b)(vii)).

Adding an AI reply-suggestion feature does not make the system high-risk; it remains outside the high-risk regime but acquires limited-risk transparency duties to the extent the suggestions are machine-generated text. Neither route to high-risk classification is engaged. Under Article 6(1) a system is high-risk only where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I and required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation; an email spam filter and reply generator is not such a product, since Annex I covers machinery, toys, recreational craft, lifts, ATEX equipment, radio equipment, pressure equipment, cableways, PPE, gas appliances, medical devices, in vitro diagnostic devices, civil aviation security, two- and three-wheel vehicles, agricultural vehicles, marine equipment, rail interoperability, motor vehicles, vehicle general safety and civil aviation. Under Article 6(2) a system is high-risk if it falls within Annex III, whose eight areas are biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and workers' management, access to essential private and public services and benefits, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes. Sorting junk mail and drafting replies for a business fits none of these, so the Article 6(3) derogation and the accompanying Article 6(4) documentation and Article 49(2) registration duties never arise. Nothing in the eight practices prohibited by Article 5(1) is engaged either. The reply-generation feature does bring Article 50 into play. As provider the operator must ensure that outputs constituting synthetic text are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, with the technical solutions effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible; this does not apply where the system performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the deployer's input data or its semantics, or where the system is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences (Article 50(2)). If the system also interacts directly with natural persons, for example an auto-responder facing the sender, Article 50(1) requires that they be informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect natural person taking into account the circumstances and context of use, and subject to the same law-enforcement carve-out. Any such information must be given clearly and distinguishably at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure, in accordance with applicable accessibility requirements (Article 50(5)). The deepfake and public-interest-text disclosure duties in Article 50(4) fall on deployers and do not attach to ordinary business correspondence.

Yes, it is a prohibited AI practice, not merely a high-risk system. Article 5(1)(g) prohibits the placing on the market, the putting into service for that specific purpose, or the use of biometric categorisation systems that categorise individually natural persons on the basis of their biometric data to deduce or infer their race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation. Inferring religious beliefs and political opinions from biometric data for ad targeting falls squarely within that list, and the prohibition binds you as a user of the system just as it binds the provider; commercial marketing is not a recognised justification, and the Regulation attaches no consent-based or legitimate-interest gateway to Article 5. The only carve-outs in point (g) are the labelling or filtering of lawfully acquired biometric datasets, such as images, on the basis of biometric data, and the categorising of biometric data in the area of law enforcement. Neither covers an ad-targeting deployment: the operator is not merely labelling or filtering a lawfully acquired dataset but individually categorising live users to infer protected attributes, and the operator is not a law enforcement actor. Because the practice is prohibited, the high-risk regime does not provide an alternative compliance route for it. Annex III, point 1(b) does classify AI systems intended for biometric categorisation according to sensitive or protected attributes based on the inference of those attributes as high-risk under Article 6(2), but that classification only operates "in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law"; where the inferred attributes are those listed in Article 5(1)(g), the Article 5 ban displaces any question of conformity assessment, registration or fundamental-rights assessment. Conversely, if you were to confine the system to biometric categorisation by sensitive or protected attributes outside the Article 5(1)(g) list, it would remain high-risk under Annex III, point 1(b), triggering the provider obligations in Article 16 (including Article 10 data governance, Article 13 instructions for use, Article 15 accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, and Article 49 EU-database registration), the deployer duties in Article 26 (use per instructions, human oversight by competent and trained persons, monitoring and incident notification under Article 26(5), and log retention for at least six months under Article 26(6)), and, by Article 26(11), the Article 50(3) duty to inform the persons exposed to the biometric categorisation system of its operation. Finally, the prohibition is triggered by the biometric inference, not by audience segmentation as such: grouping users purely by interests they have themselves stated, with no processing of biometric data, is outside both Article 5(1)(g) and Annex III, point 1(b). The compliant course is to remove the biometric inference layer from the targeting pipeline entirely.

Under the AI Act you do not register with a national regulator: registration is an entry in the EU database for high-risk AI systems, which the Commission sets up and maintains in collaboration with the Member States and for which the Commission is the controller (Article 71(1) and (6)). The provider or, where applicable, the authorised representative must register itself and the system in that database before the system is placed on the market or put into service (Article 49(1)), and the same duty applies where the provider has self-assessed an Annex III system as not high-risk under Article 6(3) (Articles 6(4) and 49(2)); this is the provider obligation restated in Article 16(1)(i). Providers established in third countries discharge it through their Union authorised representative, whose mandate must empower it to comply with the Article 49(1) registration obligations or, where the provider registers itself, to ensure the Annex VIII Section A point 3 information is correct (Article 22(1) and (3)(e)). A deployer that is a public authority, Union institution, body, office or agency, or a person acting on their behalf, must separately register itself, select the system and register its use in the same database before putting it into service or using it (Article 49(3)). Providers and authorised representatives enter the Annex VIII Section A and B data; public-authority deployers enter the Section C data (Article 71(2) and (3)). Two carve-outs change the venue or the visibility. First, high-risk systems under point 2 of Annex III (critical infrastructure) are excluded from the Article 49(1) and (3) database duties and are instead registered at national level (Article 49(5)), that is the only case in which a national authority, rather than the EU database, is the point of registration, and the Regulation leaves the designation of that national body to national implementation. Second, for systems under points 1, 6 and 7 of Annex III (biometrics, migration, asylum and border control management, and law enforcement), registration under Article 49(1), (2) and (3) is made in a secure non-public section of the EU database and is limited to Annex VIII Section A points 1 to 10 excluding points 6, 8 and 9; Annex VIII Section B points 1 to 5 and points 8 and 9; Annex VIII Section C points 1 to 3; and Annex IX points 1, 2, 3 and 5, with access restricted to the Commission and the national authorities referred to in Article 74(8) (Article 49(4)). Registration is distinct from conformity assessment: the body that may be involved in assessing the system is a notified body listed by the Commission with a single identification number (Article 35(1) and (2)), not the registration authority. Failure to comply with the registration obligation is a breach of Article 16 exposed to administrative fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, and up to the lower of those figures for SMEs and start-ups (Article 99(4)(a) and (6)); the corresponding authorised-representative failure falls under Article 99(4)(b).

No, a completed GDPR Article 35 DPIA does not discharge the AI Act's fundamental rights impact assessment; where Article 27 applies, a FRIA is still required, and the two instruments sit alongside each other. Article 27(4) is explicit that where any of the Article 27 obligations are already met through a data protection impact assessment under Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (or Article 27 of Directive (EU) 2016/680), the FRIA "shall complement" that DPIA. That is a gap-filling rule, not an exemption: the operator's DPO's DPIA can be re-used for the overlapping content, but the deployer must still produce and hold a FRIA covering the Article 27(1) elements that a DPIA does not address. Whether you owe a FRIA at all turns on Article 27(1): the duty falls on deployers of a high-risk AI system referred to in Article 6(2) (an Annex III listed use-case) that are bodies governed by public law or private entities providing public services, plus any deployer, public or private, of the Annex III point 5(b) creditworthiness/credit-scoring systems or the Annex III point 5(c) life and health insurance risk-assessment and pricing systems. It does not apply to high-risk systems intended to be used in the Annex III point 2 critical-infrastructure area (safety components in the management and operation of critical digital infrastructure, road traffic, or the supply of water, gas, heating or electricity), and it does not attach to Annex I product-route high-risk systems at all. Where it does apply, the assessment must be performed prior to deployment and must set out: (a) the deployer's processes in which the system will be used in line with its intended purpose; (b) the period of time within which, and the frequency with which, the system is intended to be used; (c) the categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected in the specific context; (d) the specific risks of harm likely to have an impact on those categories; (e) the implementation of human oversight measures, according to the instructions for use; and (f) the measures to be taken if those risks materialise, including internal governance arrangements and complaint mechanisms. Under Article 27(2) the obligation attaches to the first use, the deployer may in similar cases rely on previously conducted FRIAs or on existing impact assessments carried out by the provider, and must update the information if any element changes or is no longer up to date. Article 27(3) then adds a step with no GDPR analogue: once performed, the deployer must notify the market surveillance authority of the results, submitting the filled-out template, save where deployers may be exempt from that notification in the case referred to in Article 46(1). The AI Office is to develop that template, including through an automated tool, under Article 27(5). Practically, the DPO's DPIA can be extended rather than duplicated, mapping its processing description, affected-persons and risk sections onto Article 27(1)(a), (d), but the human-oversight description, the materialisation-response and complaints arrangements, and the authority notification must be added. The obligation applies from 2 August 2026 under Article 113(2).

The AI Act's own window is the three-month objection period in Article 79(8): where a market surveillance authority has taken a provisional measure under Article 79(5) and notified it, the measure is deemed justified if, within three months of receipt of that notification, no objection has been raised by either a market surveillance authority of another Member State or the Commission. That three-month period is reduced to 30 days where the non-compliance concerns the prohibited AI practices referred to in Article 5 (Article 79(8)). Expiry of the window is without prejudice to the concerned operator's procedural rights under Article 18 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020, and a measure deemed justified is then carried through as Union-wide restrictive action. Two adjacent periods sit upstream of it and should not be confused with it: under Article 79(2) the authority sets the period within which the operator must take corrective action, that period being proportionate to the risk rather than a fixed statutory figure; and under Articles 79(3), (5) and (7) the notification and information duties to the Commission and the other Member States run "without undue delay", not on a fixed count of days. Objections from other authorities must likewise be communicated without undue delay under Article 79(7), and restrictive measures under Article 79(9), withdrawal of the product or AI system from the market, are to be taken without undue delay.

Because fine-tuning the system on the operator's own hiring data is a substantial modification within the meaning of Article 25(1)(b), you now assume, in addition to the deployer duties you already bear, the full set of provider obligations for that specific Annex III, point 4 high-risk system, and the initial provider ceases to be its provider (Article 25(2)). As provider the operator must establish, implement, document and maintain a risk-management system run as a continuous iterative process over the entire lifecycle, comprising identification and analysis of known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety and fundamental rights in intended use, estimation and evaluation of risks in intended use and under reasonably foreseeable misuse, evaluation of other risks from post-market monitoring data, and adoption of appropriate and targeted risk-management measures, with testing against pre-determined metrics (Article 9(1), (9)); because the modification is a retraining on the operator's recruitment data, Article 10 now binds you directly: the training, validation and testing data sets must meet the quality criteria and the data-governance practices covering design choices, collection processes and data origin, preparation operations, assumptions, availability/quantity/suitability assessment, examination for possible biases affecting health, safety or fundamental rights or producing prohibited discrimination, measures to detect, prevent and mitigate such biases, and identification of relevant data gaps (Article 10(2), (4)), with Article 10(5) allowing exceptional processing of special categories of personal data strictly for bias detection and correction only where the listed cumulative conditions are met. The operator must draw up the technical documentation per Annex IV before the modified system is placed on the market or put into service and keep it up to date (Article 11(1)); ensure automatic recording of logs of events relevant to risk identification, post-market monitoring and substantial modification, retained for at least six months (Article 12); design the system for sufficient operational transparency and supply instructions for use containing provider identity and contact details, and the system's characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance, intended purpose; level of accuracy including metrics, robustness and cybersecurity against which it was tested and validated and circumstances affecting them; known or foreseeable circumstances in intended use or reasonably foreseeable misuse that may lead to risks to health, safety or fundamental rights; technical capabilities to explain output; performance regarding specific persons or groups; input-data specifications and information on the training, validation and testing data sets; and information enabling deployers to interpret the output (Article 13(1), (3)); build in effective human-oversight measures enabling the overseer to understand capacities and limitations, remain aware of automation bias, correctly interpret output, decide not to use the system or to disregard, override or reverse its output, and to intervene or stop it (Article 14); and ensure appropriate accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity throughout the lifecycle, with accuracy levels and metrics declared in the instructions (Article 15). Organisationally, the operator must operate a quality management system covering, inter alia, the regulatory-compliance strategy, design and design-verification techniques, examination and test procedures, data-management systems and procedures, post-market monitoring and incident reporting (Article 17(1)); subject the modified system to a fresh conformity assessment, the Annex VI internal-control procedure where harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied (Article 43(1), (4)); draw up the written, machine-readable, signed and dated EU declaration of conformity with the Annex V content (Article 47); affix the CE marking visibly, legibly and indelibly, or on packaging or accompanying documentation for digital-only systems (Article 48); and register yourself and the system in the EU database before placing it on the market or putting it into service (Article 49). Post-market, the operator must establish a post-market monitoring system and plan feeding back into the risk-management system (Article 72), and report serious incidents to the market-surveillance authority of the Member State where the incident occurred, immediately and in any event within two days of awareness for widespread infringement or disruption of critical infrastructure, within ten days of death, and within fifteen days for other serious incidents, or immediately once a causal link is established or reasonably likely (Article 73). The operator's existing deployer duties survive unchanged, since you continue to use the system: use per instructions, competent and trained human oversight, input-data relevance, monitoring and suspension plus incident notification, log retention, worker information before putting into service, informing the natural persons subject to the decisions, use of Article 13 information for a data protection impact assessment where applicable, and cooperation with authorities (Article 26(1), (12)); the Article 27 fundamental rights impact assessment obligation, and its notification of results to the market-surveillance authority, applies only if you fall within the categories of deployer listed in Article 27(1) and is not altered by the flip. Article 4 AI-literacy measures continue to apply to the operator in both capacities. Article 50 transparency adds provider duties only if the system directly interacts with natural persons or generates synthetic audio, image, video or text content, and in any event does not affect the Chapter III requirements (Article 50(1), (2), (6)). Finally, the initial provider must cooperate closely with you and make available the necessary information and reasonably expected technical access and assistance, in particular for the conformity assessment, unless it had clearly specified that its system was not to be changed into a high-risk AI system, subject to intellectual property rights, confidential business information and trade secrets (Article 25(2), (5)).

The operator is both: the provider and the deployer of that system, simultaneously. The operator is a provider because the operator develops the AI system and put it into service under the operator's own name for the operator's own use. The Regulation's trigger is "placing on the market or putting into service", and putting into service expressly covers supply for own use in the Union for its intended purpose; there is no internal-use or captive-deployment carve-out. "Never released externally" therefore removes none of the provider obligations, only the pre-market research and development activity itself sits outside the Regulation, and that shelter ends at the moment the system goes live in HR operations. The operator is simultaneously a deployer because you use the system under the operator's own authority in the course of a professional activity. Article 25 is not what makes you a provider here (you built it), but it would independently confirm provider status if the system is in fact a third party's model or system on which the operator puts the operator's name, which you substantially modify, or whose intended purpose you change. The practical consequence is the classification of the use. HR uses, recruitment or selection (targeted job advertising, filtering applications, evaluating candidates), decisions on promotion, termination, allocation of tasks based on behaviour or personal traits, and monitoring or evaluating performance and behaviour, are listed in Annex III, point 4, so the system is high-risk unless it genuinely falls outside those listed uses. On that basis you carry the full provider set: the risk-management system (Article 9), data governance for training, validation and testing sets (Article 10), Annex IV technical documentation before putting into service (Article 11), automatic logging (Article 12), transparency and instructions for use (Article 13), human oversight by design (Article 14), accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity (Article 15), a quality management system (Article 17), conformity assessment by internal control (Article 43), the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47), CE marking, on the documentation or packaging for a digital-only system (Article 48), registration in the EU database before putting into service (Article 49), post-market monitoring (Article 72) and serious-incident reporting (Article 73). In the operator's deployer capacity, Article 26 adds use in accordance with the instructions, human oversight assigned to competent, trained and supported natural persons, input-data relevance, monitoring with suspension and provider notification where risk arises, retention of logs under the operator's control for at least six months, information to workers' representatives and affected workers before putting the system into use, and information to persons subject to its decisions. Article 27 does not apply to the operator: the fundamental rights impact assessment binds only deployers that are bodies governed by public law, private entities providing public services, and deployers of the creditworthiness and life/health-insurance systems in Annex III, points 5(b) and (c), a private employer running HR tooling is outside that list, though the operator's provider-side risk-management and data-protection duties remain unaffected. Independently of risk class, Article 4 requires AI literacy measures for the operator's staff in both capacities, Article 5's prohibitions apply regardless of internal use, relevant here for emotion inference in the workplace, and, if the system interacts with the operator's staff or generates synthetic text, Article 50(1) and 50(2) require disclosure of its AI nature and machine-readable marking of outputs, subject to their carve-outs for what is obvious to a reasonably well-informed person, for systems performing an assistive editing function or not substantially altering the input data or its semantics, and for uses authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences; Article 50(6) leaves the Chapter III high-risk requirements untouched.

Putting the operator's own name or trademark on a high-risk AI system that has already been placed on the market or put into service makes you the provider of that system, and you assume the full set of provider obligations under Article 16 (Article 25(1)(a)). That conversion is triggered by the re-branding alone, no technical change is required, and it applies without prejudice to contractual arrangements stipulating that the obligations are otherwise allocated between you and the original provider. The same conversion occurs, on the exhaustive list in Article 25(1), where you make a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system already on the market such that it remains high-risk under Article 6 (point (b)), or where you modify the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, not previously classified as high-risk so that it becomes high-risk under Article 6 (point (c)). If the system you re-brand is not high-risk and you do not alter its intended purpose so as to make it high-risk, Article 25(1) does not convert you into a provider of a high-risk system, though Article 50 transparency duties and Article 4 AI literacy duties still bind you as provider or deployer, and the Article 5 prohibitions apply irrespective of role. On conversion, the original provider ceases to be the provider of that specific AI system, but must cooperate closely with you and make available the necessary information and the reasonably expected technical access and other assistance required for you to fulfil the obligations of this Regulation, in particular compliance with the conformity assessment (Article 25(2)); this does not apply where the initial provider has clearly specified that its system is not to be changed into a high-risk AI system. A distinct allocation applies under Article 25(3) where the high-risk system is a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I: the product manufacturer is the provider where the system is placed on the market together with the product under the manufacturer's name or trademark (Article 25(3)(a)), or is put into service under that name or trademark after the product has been placed on the market (Article 25(3)(b)). Paragraphs 2 and 3 are without prejudice to the protection of trade secrets (Article 25(5)). Practically, before you sell the re-branded system on the operator must, in the operator's own name: operate a documented, continuous risk management system across the lifecycle, including identification and analysis of foreseeable risks, estimation of risks under intended purpose and reasonably foreseeable misuse, evaluation of risks from post-market data, and adoption of targeted risk management measures (Article 9(1), (2)); satisfy the data-governance requirements for training, validation and testing data sets, covering design choices, collection processes and data origin, preparation operations, assumptions, availability and suitability assessment, bias examination, bias mitigation measures, and data-gap identification (Article 10(2)); draw up and keep up to date Annex IV technical documentation before placing the system on the market (Article 11(1)); ensure automatic logging with retention of at least six months (Article 12); design for transparency and supply instructions for use identifying you as provider (Article 13); build in and specify human-oversight measures, both those built into the system by the provider and those identified by the provider as appropriate for the deployer to implement (Article 14(3)(a) and (b)); meet accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity requirements and declare accuracy metrics (Article 15); operate a quality management system (Article 17); complete the applicable conformity assessment (Article 43); draw up the signed, dated, machine-readable EU declaration of conformity with the Annex V content (Article 47); affix the CE marking visibly, legibly and indelibly, with the notified body's identification number where applicable (Article 48); and register yourself and the system in the EU database before placing it on the market, except for Annex III point 2 systems (Article 49(1)). Where you conclude under Article 6(3) that a listed system is not high-risk, the operator must still register yourself and that system before placing it on the market (Article 49(2)). After sale, the provider-side post-market duties are yours: a documented post-market monitoring plan and system feeding back into the risk management system (Article 72), and serious-incident reporting to the market surveillance authority of the Member State where the incident occurred, immediately and in any event within two days of awareness for widespread infringement or disruption of critical infrastructure, within ten days of awareness for death, and within fifteen days for other serious incidents, or immediately upon establishing the causal link (Article 73). You also owe AI literacy measures for the operator's staff and others operating the system on the operator's behalf (Article 4), and, where the system interacts directly with natural persons, must ensure they are informed they are interacting with an AI system unless that is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person in the circumstances, an exception that does not extend to systems merely authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences where those systems are available for the public to report an offence, with that information given clearly and distinguishably at the latest at the time of first interaction and in conformity with applicable accessibility requirements (Article 50(1), (5)). If you also continue to use the system yourself, the deployer duties in Articles 26 and, where applicable, the fundamental rights impact assessment in Article 27 remain separately owed.

No, a pre‑training run reaching exactly 1×10²⁵ FLOPs does not, by itself, change the model's classification under Article 51. The presumption of high‑impact capabilities in Article 51(2) is triggered only where the cumulative amount of computation used for the model's training, measured in floating point operations, is greater than 10²⁵ FLOPs; a figure that merely reaches, but does not exceed, that value falls outside the presumption. Two further qualifiers matter: the metric is cumulative training compute for the model, not the pre‑training stage in isolation, so pre‑training FLOPs must be aggregated with the rest of the training computation before the threshold is tested; and the threshold is only a presumption route into Article 51(1), point (b). Classification as a general‑purpose AI model with systemic risk can still arise independently under Article 51(1), point (a), where the model has high‑impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools, methodologies, indicators and benchmarks, or by Commission decision, ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel, on the basis of the Annex XIII criteria (number of parameters, quality or size of the dataset, amount of computation used for training, input and output modalities, benchmarks and capability evaluations, reach including number of business users and registered EU end‑users). Absent systemic‑risk designation, the operator's obligations as provider remain those in Article 53(1): drawing up and keeping up to date the technical documentation containing at a minimum the Annex XI information, for provision on request to the AI Office and national competent authorities (Article 53(1), point (a)); drawing up, keeping up to date and making available to downstream providers information enabling them to understand the model's capabilities and limitations and to comply with their own obligations, containing at a minimum the Annex XII elements (Article 53(1), point (b), subpoints (i) and (ii)); putting in place a policy to comply with Union copyright law, including identifying and complying, through state‑of‑the‑art technologies, with a rights reservation expressed under Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790 (Article 53(1), point (c)); and making publicly available a sufficiently detailed summary of the training content per the AI Office template (Article 53(1), point (d)). Note that the compute figure itself is a documentation item in any event: Annex XI, point 2(d) requires the computational resources used to train the model, expressed for example as number of floating point operations, together with training time and, under point 2(e), known or estimated energy consumption, which may be derived from the compute information where unknown. Two limitations on that documentation set bear on the operator's position. Under Article 53(2), points (a) and (b) of paragraph 1 do not apply to models released under a free and open‑source licence permitting access, use, modification and distribution, with parameters including weights, model architecture information and model usage information publicly available, but that exception is expressly unavailable to general‑purpose AI models with systemic risk, so it would be lost if the model were ultimately classified under Article 51. Under Article 53(4), you may rely on codes of practice within the meaning of Article 56 to demonstrate compliance with paragraph 1 until a harmonised standard is published, with a presumption of conformity for compliance with European harmonised standards to the extent they cover those obligations, failing which the operator must demonstrate alternative adequate means of compliance for Commission assessment. The unresolved condition is therefore arithmetical and factual rather than legal: if total training computation for the model in fact exceeds 10²⁵ FLOPs, or if it is reasonably foreseeable that it will, the Article 51(2) presumption engages and the systemic‑risk regime attaches on top of Article 53.

No, a training run of 3.3×10²⁴ FLOPs does not, of itself, make you a provider. The "one third of the original model's training compute" figure is not a threshold in Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as adopted; it originates in Commission-level guidance and codes, which are interpretive aids and do not independently create a statutory duty or a status change. Hitting it "exactly" therefore has no operative legal effect on the face of the Regulation. The only compute-linked mechanism in the adopted text runs to the classification of a general-purpose AI model as presenting systemic risk, where training compute sits alongside parameter count, dataset quality and size, input and output modalities, benchmark and capability evaluations, reach among business users and EU-registered end-users, and registered users (Annex XIII). That is a question about a model's risk tier, not about who is a provider, and the interpretive material accompanying it (Recital 112) describes only a presumption of systemic risk where the high-impact-capability threshold is met. Provider status along the value chain is determined by conduct, not by FLOPs. Under Article 25(1) a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party becomes a provider subject to the Article 16 obligations only where (a) it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service, without prejudice to contractual allocation; (b) it makes a substantial modification to such a system in such a way that it remains high-risk under Article 6; or (c) it modifies the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, not classified as high-risk, so that the system becomes high-risk under Article 6. If one of those limbs is met, the initial provider ceases to be the provider of that system, must cooperate closely and supply the necessary information, reasonably expected technical access and other assistance, unless it clearly specified that its system was not to be changed into a high-risk system (Article 25(2)), and the written-agreement duty in Article 25(4) and the intellectual-property and trade-secret reservation in Article 25(5) apply. The narrow unresolved condition is factual: whether you market the fine-tuned model or system under the operator's own name or trademark, and whether the result is high-risk under Article 6. If the operator places it on the market in the operator's own name, provider duties attach because of that act, including the Article 50(1) duty to design systems intended to interact directly with natural persons so that those persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless that is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person in the circumstances and context of use, and excepting systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences subject to appropriate safeguards, unless available to the public to report an offence, and the Article 4 AI-literacy duty, which binds providers and deployers alike.

Yes, training on 2×10²⁵ FLOPs removes the benefit of the Article 53(2) open-source carve-out, so the full documentation obligations apply despite the Apache 2.0 / open-weights release. Article 53(2) disapplies the Article 53(1)(a) technical-documentation duty and the Article 53(1)(b) downstream-information duty only for models released under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution, and whose parameters, weights, model-architecture information and model-usage information, are publicly available. That same paragraph states that the exception does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk. Because cumulative training compute of 2×10²⁵ floating point operations is greater than 10²⁵, the model is presumed under Article 51(2) to have high-impact capabilities within the meaning of Article 51(1)(a) and is therefore classified as a GPAI model with systemic risk. The licence and public weights become legally irrelevant to points (a) and (b). Consequently the operator must draw up and keep up to date the technical documentation of the model, including its training and testing process and evaluation results, containing at a minimum the Annex XI information (general description including tasks, integration paradigms, acceptable-use policies, release date and distribution methods; architecture and parameter count; modality and format; licensing; training process; data and compute used; energy consumption; evaluation results), for provision on request to the AI Office and national competent authorities (Article 53(1)(a)); and the operator must draw up, keep up to date and make available to providers of AI systems intending to integrate the model information and documentation that (i) enables them to understand the model's capabilities and limitations and to comply with their own obligations under the Regulation, and (ii) contains at a minimum the Annex XII elements, without prejudice to intellectual property rights and confidential business information or trade secrets (Article 53(1)(b)). The copyright policy under Article 53(1)(c), including identifying and complying with Article 4(3) Directive (EU) 2019/790 rights reservations through state-of-the-art technologies, and the publicly available sufficiently detailed training-content summary per the AI Office template under Article 53(1)(d), applied to you at any compute level and continue to apply. Systemic-risk classification additionally triggers Article 55(1): state-of-the-art model evaluation including documented adversarial testing (a); assessment and mitigation of possible Union-level systemic risks and their sources arising from development, placing on the market or use (b); tracking, documenting and reporting serious incidents and possible corrective measures to the AI Office and, as appropriate, national competent authorities without undue delay (c); and adequate cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure (d). You may rely on codes of practice within the meaning of Article 56 to demonstrate compliance with Article 53(1) and Article 55(1) until a harmonised standard is published, and information obtained under those Articles, including trade secrets, is protected by the confidentiality regime of Article 78 (Article 53(4), Article 53(7), Article 55(2), Article 55(3)).

Neither provision prevails: there is no conflict to resolve, because Article 13 and Article 50(1) impose cumulative duties on different information recipients, and Article 50(6) expressly provides that paragraphs 1 to 4 of Article 50 shall not affect the requirements and obligations set out in Chapter III. A medical-triage chatbot that is high-risk, whether through the Annex III route (point 5(d) covers emergency healthcare patient triage systems, and point 5(a) covers eligibility evaluation for healthcare benefits and services) or through the Annex I product route as a medical device under Regulation (EU) 2017/745, with the AI Act requirements folded into the sectoral notified-body assessment under Article 43(3), must therefore satisfy both layers in full. Article 13(1) requires the system to be designed and developed so that its operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret its output and use it appropriately, with an appropriate type and degree of transparency having regard to the provider's and deployer's Section 3 obligations (Article 13(2), which also requires concise, complete, correct and clear instructions for use that are relevant, accessible and comprehensible to deployers), and Article 13(3) fixes the content of those instructions: provider identity and contact details (point (a)); the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance (point (b)), namely intended purpose (i), level of accuracy including metrics, robustness and cybersecurity tested and validated against and circumstances affecting them (ii), known or foreseeable circumstances of intended use or reasonably foreseeable misuse that may lead to Article 9(2) risks to health, safety or fundamental rights (iii), technical capabilities to explain the output where applicable (iv), performance regarding specific persons or groups where appropriate (v), input-data specifications and training, validation and testing data information where appropriate (vi), and information enabling deployers to interpret and appropriately use the output where applicable (vii); pre-determined changes and performance (point (c)); the human-oversight measures (point (d)); computational and hardware resources and expected lifetime plus required maintenance and care measures (point (e)); and, where relevant, the log-collection, storage and interpretation mechanisms under Article 12 (point (f)). Article 50(1) runs to a different addressee, the natural person interacting with the chatbot, and obliges the provider to design and develop the system so that the person is informed that they are interacting with an AI system. That duty carries only two carve-outs: where the AI nature is obvious from the point of view of a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect natural person, taking into account the circumstances and context of use; and for AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards for third parties' rights and freedoms, unless those systems are available for the public to report a criminal offence. Neither carve-out is ordinarily available to a patient-facing triage chatbot: the law-enforcement exemption is off-purpose, and obviousness cannot be assumed for a conversational clinical interface used by patients who may be distressed or vulnerable. Under Article 50(5) the information must be given in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure, and must conform to the applicable accessibility requirements. The same additive logic applies at deployer level: Article 26(11) opens "Without prejudice to Article 50" and requires deployers of Annex III high-risk systems that make or assist in making decisions about natural persons to inform those persons that they are subject to the use of the high-risk system, alongside the Article 26(1) duty to use the system in accordance with the instructions for use supplied under Article 13. Practically, the provider discharges Article 13 through the instructions-for-use and design documentation delivered to the health institution, and discharges Article 50(1) through an in-product disclosure at the opening of the interaction; providing information to the deployer under Article 13(3) is also one of the Article 9(5)(c) risk-control measures and does not substitute for the end-user disclosure. Compliance with one layer is not a defence to the other, and the disclosure design must be tested and judged as part of the Article 9 risk-management system, with residual risks communicated to the deployer under Article 9(6).

No, at 250 employees and €60 million turnover you no longer qualify for the priority access in Article 62(1)(a), and that benefit does not carry over from the operator's earlier size. Article 62(1)(a) requires Member States to give priority access to the AI regulatory sandboxes to SMEs, including start-ups, having a registered office or a branch in the Union, and only to the extent that they fulfil the eligibility conditions and selection criteria. The entitlement is attached to the operator's current status as an SME, not vested at first accession and not grandfathered; the Regulation uses the SME definition of Commission Recommendation 2003/361/EC, whose ceilings are fewer than 250 staff together with turnover not exceeding €50 million or a balance-sheet total not exceeding €43 million. Both of the operator's figures breach those ceilings, so the SME-specific treatment lapses once the change of status takes effect, under that Recommendation, status is lost only where the thresholds are exceeded in two consecutive accounting periods, and the staff and turnover data of any partner or linked enterprises must be consolidated, so the precise date of loss is the one narrow point the operator must verify against the operator's own accounts. Losing the priority does not lose you the sandbox. Access itself is not reserved to SMEs: Article 57(1) obliges each Member State to ensure a national sandbox, and Article 57(5) opens the controlled environment to providers and prospective providers under a specific sandbox plan agreed with the competent authority; Article 62(1)(a) expressly states only that priority shall not preclude other SMEs, including start-ups, from access where they meet the eligibility conditions and selection criteria. You therefore apply on ordinary terms, ranked without precedence, and retain the full sandbox benefits once admitted, guidance and supervision under Article 57(6), written proof of activities and an exit report under Article 57(7), and the no-administrative-fines protection in Article 57(12) where you observe the sandbox plan and follow the authority's guidance in good faith. The other Article 62(1) measures follow the same logic: the tailored awareness-raising and training in point (b) and the dedicated communication channels in point (c) are directed at SMEs including start-ups and at deployers, so you may still use them in the operator's deployer capacity, while the facilitation of participation in standardisation in point (d) extends to SMEs and other relevant stakeholders and so remains open to you. The fee mitigation in Article 62(2), reduction of conformity assessment fees under Article 43 proportionate to size, market size and other relevant indicators, is confined to SME providers including start-ups and ceases with the operator's SME status. The AI Office actions in Article 62(3), including the standardised templates and the single information platform, are addressed to all operators across the Union and are unaffected by the operator's growth. An ongoing sandbox participation already granted is governed by the operator's agreed plan and may be suspended only on the risk grounds in Article 57(11), not because you have outgrown the SME thresholds.

Yes, if the tool infers emotions of call‑centre agents from their biometric data, placing it on the market for that purpose, putting it into service for that purpose, and the call centre's use of it are all prohibited by Article 5(1)(f), which bans AI systems to infer emotions of a natural person in the areas of workplace and education institutions. A commercial call centre is a workplace and the agents are workers within that area, so the prohibition bites on the provider at the point of placing on the market or putting into service for this specific purpose, and independently on the deployer at the point of use; no employee consent or works‑council agreement cures it. Article 5(1)(f) carries one carve‑out: systems intended to be put in place or into the market for medical or safety reasons. Monitoring stress to manage workload, quality or productivity is not covered; the carve‑out reaches genuine health‑protection or accident‑prevention purposes, and Recital 44 signals that it is to be read narrowly given the power imbalance in the employment context. Two definitional limits may take the tool outside Article 5(1)(f) altogether. First, the system must identify or infer emotions on the basis of biometric data; a tool working solely on call transcripts, handling‑time or ticket metadata is not an emotion recognition system. Second, Recital 18 excludes physical states such as pain or fatigue, so a purely physiological fatigue or arousal indicator may fall outside, whereas inferring states such as anger, frustration or embarrassment does not. If either limit applies, the system is not prohibited but falls to be assessed under Article 6(2) with Annex III, points 1(c) and 4(b), and to the deployer information duty in Article 50(3).

No. Adding ethnicity inference for marketing personalisation is not permitted, it falls squarely within the prohibition in Article 5(1), point (g), which bars the placing on the market, the putting into service for that specific purpose, or the use of biometric categorisation systems that categorise individually natural persons on the basis of their biometric data to deduce or infer their race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation. The operator's tool would assign individual shoppers to categories from facial or other biometric data (Article 3(34), Article 3(40)), and inferring ethnicity from such data is an inference of race within the meaning of point (g), as Recital 30 confirms in describing deduction of race from an individual's face or fingerprint. The commercial or "personalisation" motive is irrelevant: point (g) is a use prohibition with no legitimate-interest, consent or marketing justification, and it binds provider and deployer alike. Neither of the two carve-outs written into point (g) rescues the use case. The first excludes any labelling or filtering of lawfully acquired biometric datasets, such as images, based on biometric data, i.e. offline dataset curation such as sorting images by hair or eye colour (Recital 30), not live individual categorisation of shoppers by a protected attribute. The second excludes categorising of biometric data in the area of law enforcement, which a retail analytics deployment plainly is not. The definitional exclusion in Article 3(40), a system is not a biometric categorisation system where the categorisation is ancillary to another commercial service and strictly necessary for objective technical reasons, is also unavailable: ethnicity labels for marketing personalisation are the commercial purpose itself and are not technically necessary to deliver any underlying service. The existing age-range function is not caught by Article 5(1)(g), since age is not among the attributes it enumerates, but it remains a biometric categorisation system according to protected attributes inferred from biometric data and is therefore high-risk under Annex III, point 1(b) via Article 6(2), with the Article 6(3) derogation unavailable where the system profiles natural persons. That entails, among others, the provider duties of transparency and instructions for use under Article 13(1)-(3), human oversight designed in under Article 14, conformity assessment under Article 43 with registration under Article 49(1), and the deployer's duty under Article 50(3) to inform the natural persons exposed to the system of its operation and to process personal data in accordance with Regulations (EU) 2016/679 and (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680, a duty that is disapplied only for biometric categorisation and emotion recognition permitted by law to detect, prevent or investigate criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards. The ethnicity feature should be dropped from the design rather than mitigated, because no downstream safeguard can make a prohibited practice lawful.

Under Article 5.1.h, real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces by law-enforcement authorities is prohibited; narrow exceptions require prior judicial or independent-administrative authorization, an Article 27 fundamental-rights impact assessment, and Article 49 EU-database registration. Real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces by law enforcement is prohibited under Article 5(1)(h), with narrow exceptions for victim searches, imminent or terrorist threats, and locating serious-crime suspects. Real-time remote biometric identification by law enforcement is prohibited under Article 5 save for narrow, exhaustively-listed law-enforcement exceptions that each require prior judicial or administrative authorisation; under Article 5(5) Member States may enable those exceptions in national law and may set stricter national rules. Article 5(1)(c) carve-out: the social-scoring prohibition does not affect lawful evaluation practices of natural persons that are carried out for a specific purpose in accordance with Union and national law (Recital 31 final sentence). Article 5(1)(g) carve-out: the biometric-categorisation prohibition does not cover lawful labelling, filtering or categorisation of biometric datasets acquired in line with Union or national law, including sorting by hair colour or eye colour, which is permitted in law-enforcement contexts (Recital 30). Article 5(1)(h) carve-out catalogue: real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces by law enforcement is permitted only for three exhaustive law-enforcement objectives, (i) targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking and sexual exploitation, and missing persons; (ii) prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety, or a genuine and foreseeable terrorist attack; (iii) localisation or identification of suspects of Annex II offences punishable by at least 4 years' custody. Use requires prior FRIA (Article 27), Article 49 EU-database registration, prior judicial or independent-administrative authorisation (urgency exception: authorisation within 24h, else immediate stop), and notification of the relevant market-surveillance authority and national data-protection authority. Article 5(1)(b) coverage for minors: the vulnerability-exploitation prohibition expressly captures AI systems that exploit vulnerabilities arising from age, minors in particular. Compliance pathways include age-appropriate design, robust age-estimation safeguards proportionate to the risk to children, and the Article 50 transparency duties where the system interacts with users directly.

Using the system to select employees for redundancy keeps it high-risk, indeed it moves it to the core of the same use-case. Annex III(4)(b) covers AI systems intended to be used to make decisions affecting terms of work-related relationships and, expressly, the termination of work-related contractual relationships, alongside task allocation based on individual behaviour or personal traits and the monitoring and evaluation of performance and behaviour of persons in such relationships. A redundancy-selection use therefore engages both limbs of that point: the performance-evaluation limb you already relied on, and the termination-decision limb. Under Article 6(2), an AI system referred to in Annex III is high-risk, so the change of purpose does not alter the classification, it reinforces it. The Article 6(3) derogation is not realistically available here. It applies only where the system poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making, and only where one of four conditions is met: (a) a narrow procedural task; (b) improving the result of a previously completed human activity; (c) detecting decision-making patterns or deviations from prior patterns without being meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment, absent proper human review; or (d) a preparatory task to an assessment relevant to an Annex III use-case. A system whose scores drive who is dismissed materially influences the outcome, and in any event Article 6(3), second subparagraph, provides that an Annex III system is always high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons, which scoring individual employees on performance will ordinarily constitute. Should a provider nonetheless take the view that the system is not high-risk, Article 6(4) requires that assessment to be documented before placing on the market or putting into service, brings the provider within the registration obligation in Article 49(2), and requires the documentation to be produced to national competent authorities on request. One practical consequence: repurposing the system from performance evaluation to redundancy selection changes its intended purpose, so the classification, documentation and conformity position must be revisited for that new purpose rather than carried over from the original one.

No, you cannot deploy the system to a real client as a live hiring tool during the sandbox phase. An AI regulatory sandbox is a controlled environment for the development, training, testing and validation of innovative AI systems for a limited time before they are placed on the market or put into service, pursuant to a specific sandbox plan agreed with the competent authority (Article 57(5)); placing the high-risk system on the market or putting it into service for a client's actual recruitment decisions falls outside the sandbox and triggers the full high-risk regime, including conformity assessment and CE marking, with no sandbox derogation. What is permitted is testing with a real client, in two forms. First, the Spanish sandbox may itself include testing in real world conditions supervised therein (Article 57(5)), under the guidance, supervision and support of the competent authority aimed at identifying risks to fundamental rights, health and safety and at verifying mitigation measures (Article 57(6)). Second, you may conduct testing in real world conditions outside the sandbox under Article 60, at any time before placing on the market or putting into service, alone or in partnership with one or more deployers or prospective deployers (Article 60(1) and (2)), a hiring system being an Annex III listed use. Article 60 testing is lawful only where all of the following conditions are met (Article 60(4)): a real-world testing plan drawn up and submitted to the market surveillance authority of the Member State of testing; approval by that authority of both the testing and the plan, with tacit approval after 30 days unless national law requires express authorisation; registration of the testing under Article 71(4) with a Union-wide unique single identification number and the information in Annex IX (the law-enforcement, migration and biometrics derogations in that point do not apply to a hiring system); establishment of the provider or prospective provider in the Union or appointment of a Union-established legal representative; transfer of data to third countries only with appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law; a duration no longer than necessary and in any event not exceeding six months, extendable once by six months on prior reasoned notification to the market surveillance authority; appropriate protection of subjects belonging to vulnerable groups due to age or disability; where testing is organised with a deployer or prospective deployer, prior information to that deployer of all aspects relevant to its decision to participate, provision of the instructions for use, and a concluded agreement specifying the parties' roles and responsibilities; informed consent of the testing subjects (with the narrow law-enforcement alternative of no negative effect plus deletion of personal data, which is unavailable here); effective oversight by the provider and the deployer through suitably qualified persons with the necessary capacity, training and authority; and the capacity to effectively reverse and disregard the system's predictions, recommendations or decisions. Testing subjects may withdraw consent at any time without detriment or justification and request immediate and permanent deletion of their personal data, without affecting activities already carried out (Article 60(5)). The testing is without prejudice to any ethical review required by Union or national law (Article 60(3)) and to the prohibitions in Article 5 (Article 60(1)). During Article 60 testing the market surveillance authority may require information, carry out unannounced remote or on-site inspections and check the conduct of the testing (Article 60(6)); any serious incident must be reported to that authority under Article 73, with immediate mitigation or otherwise suspension or termination and a procedure for prompt recall (Article 60(7)); and suspension, termination and final outcomes must be notified to it (Article 60(8)). Liability for damage caused in the course of testing remains with the provider or prospective provider (Article 60(9)), as it does for damage inflicted on third parties by experimentation in the sandbox (Article 57(12)), although no administrative fines are imposed for infringements of this Regulation where the sandbox plan and participation terms are observed and the authority's guidance is followed in good faith. The competent authority retains the power to suspend the testing process or the operator's participation temporarily or permanently where significant risks to health, safety or fundamental rights cannot be effectively mitigated (Article 57(11)).

No, the EUR 35 000 000 figure is not the ceiling that applies to the operator, provided you qualify as an SME or start-up. Article 99(3) sets the Article 5 ceiling at up to EUR 35 000 000 or, for an undertaking, up to 7 % of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher; but Article 99(6) reverses that arithmetic for SMEs, including start-ups, so each fine referred to in Article 99 is capped at the percentage or the fixed amount, whichever is lower. For a 25-employee company, 7 % of worldwide annual turnover will be far below EUR 35 000 000, so 7 % of the operator's group's worldwide turnover for the preceding financial year is the operative maximum. That is a ceiling, not a tariff: Article 99(1) requires penalties to be effective, proportionate and dissuasive, having regard to the interests of SMEs, including start-ups, and their economic viability. The amount actually imposed is then set under Article 99(7), whose factors are: the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement and its consequences, taking account of the purpose of the system and the number of affected persons and the damage suffered; whether other authorities have already imposed fines for the same infringement; whether other authorities have already fined the same operator for infringements of other Union or national law; the size, annual turnover and market share of the operator; any other aggravating or mitigating factor, including financial benefits gained or losses avoided; the degree of cooperation with national competent authorities; the degree of responsibility of the operator, accounting for technical and organisational measures implemented; how the infringement became known, in particular whether the operator notified it and to what extent; the intentional or negligent character of the infringement; and any action taken by the operator to mitigate the harm suffered by affected persons. On the operator's facts, the six-month duration and the knowing character of the deployment weigh directly against you under the first and ninth of those factors, while self-notification, cooperation and mitigation are the levers that remain available.

The Annex III route applies: classification runs through Article 6(2), not the Annex I product route in Article 6(1). Article 6(1) is available only where the AI system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation; an employment or worker-management system is not classified that way unless it independently meets both of those conditions. Under Article 6(2), a system falls to be high-risk because it is one of the systems referred to in Annex III, and being "under Annex III(4)" is only half the test, point 4 is an area heading, and the system must match one of its two lettered use-cases: (a) AI systems intended to be used for the recruitment or selection of natural persons, in particular to place targeted job advertisements, to analyse and filter job applications, and to evaluate candidates; or (b) AI systems intended to be used to make decisions affecting terms of work-related relationships, the promotion or termination of work-related contractual relationships, to allocate tasks based on individual behaviour or personal traits or characteristics, or to monitor and evaluate the performance and behaviour of persons in such relationships. If the intended purpose matches neither lettered entry, Article 6(2) is not engaged. Where a lettered use-case is matched, the only exit is the Article 6(3) derogation: the system is not high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making, and one of four conditions is fulfilled, (a) it performs a narrow procedural task; (b) it improves the result of a previously completed human activity; (c) it detects decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns and is not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment without proper human review; or (d) it performs a preparatory task to an assessment relevant for an Annex III use case. That derogation is unavailable where the system performs profiling of natural persons, in which case it is always high-risk, a decisive limit for employment tools that score or rank candidates or workers on personal traits or behaviour. A provider relying on the derogation must document the assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service, is subject to the registration obligation in Article 49(2), and must provide that documentation to national competent authorities upon request (Article 6(4)).

Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as adopted, Annex I embedded high-risk systems come under the regime later than the Annex III route: Article 6(1) and the corresponding obligations of the Regulation apply from 2 August 2027 (Article 113(3)(c)), one year after the Regulation's general date of application of 2 August 2026 (Article 113(2)). That deferred date attaches to the product route in Article 6(1): an AI system is high-risk where it is either itself a product, or a safety component of a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I (Article 6(1)(a)), and that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service (Article 6(1)(b)). For medical devices this means Regulation (EU) 2017/745 and, for in vitro diagnostics, Regulation (EU) 2017/746, both listed in Annex I; the same 2 August 2027 timing applies to the other Annex I instruments, including machinery, toys, recreational craft, lifts, ATEX equipment, radio equipment, pressure equipment, cableway installations, personal protective equipment, gas appliances, and the Section B acts on civil aviation security, two- and three-wheel vehicles, agricultural and forestry vehicles, marine equipment, rail interoperability, motor vehicle type-approval, vehicle general safety, and civil aviation under Regulation (EU) 2018/1139. Two qualifiers are worth preserving. The Article 6(3) derogation, narrow procedural task, improving a previously completed human activity, detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, or a preparatory task, and in every case subject to the profiling override, derogates only from Article 6(2), so it is unavailable to an Annex I safety component; classification there turns solely on the sectoral third-party conformity assessment requirement. Separately, the obligations that are not tied to Article 6(1) run on their own earlier clocks regardless of the embedded-product deferral: the Article 5 prohibitions and the Article 4 AI literacy duty from 2 February 2025 (Article 113(3)(a)) and the general-purpose AI obligations from 2 August 2025 (Article 113(3)(b)).

No. Within Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as adopted, the version governing this assessment, none of the transitional dates have been moved, and the Digital Omnibus is a later Commission legislative initiative that forms no part of this corpus; it cannot be treated as displacing the Act's text unless and until it is adopted and enters into force. The timeline as adopted therefore stands in Article 111. AI systems that are components of the large-scale IT systems established by the legal acts listed in Annex X and placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2027 must be brought into compliance by 31 December 2030, with the Regulation's requirements taken into account when each of those systems is evaluated or its underlying act replaced or amended, and this is without prejudice to Article 5 as referred to in Article 113(3), point (a) (Article 111(1)). Operators of other high-risk AI systems placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2026 are caught only where those systems undergo significant changes in design after that date, while high-risk systems intended for use by public authorities must in any event be brought into compliance by 2 August 2030 (Article 111(2)). Providers of general-purpose AI models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 must take the necessary steps to comply by 2 August 2027 (Article 111(3)). If you need an assessment against a subsequently amended text, that has to be run against the amending instrument once adopted; on the adopted version supplied here, the deadlines are unchanged.

If you do not adhere to a code of practice under Article 56, Article 53(4) leaves you two routes. First, you may comply with a European harmonised standard: compliance with such standards grants a presumption of conformity to the extent those standards cover the Article 53(1) obligations, that is, the Annex XI technical documentation, the Annex XII downstream-provider information, the copyright policy and the public training-data summary. Second, if you neither adhere to an approved code of practice nor comply with a European harmonised standard, the operator must demonstrate alternative adequate means of compliance for assessment by the Commission (Article 53(4)). Reliance on a code of practice is itself only an interim route, available until a harmonised standard is published. Practically, the third route is self-constructed: you remain bound by the substantive Article 53(1) duties in full and must be able to put the operator's own documentation, copyright policy and training-data summary before the Commission (through the AI Office) as adequate means, without the benefit of any presumption of conformity, the burden of persuading the Commission rests on you. Note that the Article 53(2) carve-out for models released under a free and open-source licence with publicly available parameters removes only the Article 53(1)(a) and (b) documentation duties, and not for models with systemic risk; the copyright policy and training-data summary remain in all cases. If the operator's model is classified as having systemic risk under Article 51(1), including the presumption where cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 floating-point operations (Article 51(2)), the identical structure applies separately to the four Article 55(1) obligations: model evaluation with adversarial testing, assessment and mitigation of Union-level systemic risks, serious-incident tracking, documentation and reporting to the AI Office, and cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure. Under Article 55(2) you may rely on a code of practice until a harmonised standard is published, harmonised-standard compliance gives the presumption of conformity to the extent covered, and otherwise the operator must demonstrate alternative adequate means of compliance for Commission assessment. Information and documentation you submit, including trade secrets, is protected by the confidentiality obligations of Article 78 (Articles 53(7), 55(3)).

No. The AI Office has no autonomous power to impose fines on providers of general-purpose AI models; the power to fine GPAI providers is vested in the Commission, and the AI Office acts as the Commission's internal body carrying out supervisory, monitoring and evidence-gathering functions in support of that decision, not as an independent enforcement authority in its own name. That allocation is visible in the provisions governing GPAI providers themselves. The AI Office is consistently designated as a recipient of information rather than as a decision-maker: Article 53(1)(a) requires the technical documentation compiled under Annex XI to be kept up to date "for the purpose of providing it, upon request, to the AI Office and the national competent authorities", Article 53(1)(d) requires the publicly available training-content summary to follow "a template provided by the AI Office", and Article 55(1)(c) requires providers of models with systemic risk to report serious incidents and possible corrective measures without undue delay to the AI Office and, as appropriate, to national competent authorities. Anything so obtained, including trade secrets, is bound by the confidentiality regime of Article 78 (Articles 53(7) and 55(3)). Where a binding legal determination or an assessment with legal consequences is made, the Act names the Commission, not the AI Office: classification of a model as carrying systemic risk rests on a decision of the Commission, ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel, against the Annex XIII criteria (Article 51(1)(b)), alongside the compute presumption above 10^25 FLOPs in Article 51(2); providers who neither adhere to an approved code of practice under Article 56 nor comply with a harmonised standard must demonstrate alternative adequate means of compliance "for assessment by the Commission" (Articles 53(4) and 55(2)); and the power to adopt delegated acts detailing measurement methodologies and amending Annexes XI and XII lies with the Commission (Article 53(5) and (6)). The general cooperation duty in Article 53(3) is owed to the Commission and the national competent authorities in the exercise of their competences and powers under the Regulation.

The operator is conditionally grandfathered, not automatically exempt: a high-risk AI system placed on the market in March 2026, i.e. before 2 August 2026, does not have to be retrofitted to the Regulation's high-risk requirements unless one of three conditions bites (Article 111(2)). First, the grandfathering lapses if, as from 2 August 2026, the system is subject to significant changes in its design; from that point the Regulation applies to operators of the system in full, and the operator must then bring it into conformity (including Chapter III requirements, conformity assessment and CE marking) as an ordinary high-risk system (Article 111(2)). Second, the exemption is not open-ended for public-sector deployment: if the system is intended to be used by public authorities, providers and deployers must in any case take the necessary steps to comply with the requirements and obligations of the Regulation by 2 August 2030, whether or not the design changes (Article 111(2)). Third, if the system is a component of one of the large-scale IT systems established by the acts listed in SIS, VIS, Eurodac, EES, ETIAS, ECRIS-TCN and the interoperability Regulations, a different rule governs: placement before 2 August 2027 triggers a duty to bring it into compliance by 31 December 2030, and the Regulation's requirements must be taken into account in the scheduled evaluation of each such system and where those acts are replaced or amended (Article 111(1), Annex X). Two limits on the relief should be noted. It is expressed "without prejudice to the application of Article 5", so the prohibited-practice ban applies from its own date regardless of when the system was placed on the market (Article 111(1) and (2)).
